speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition the other morning asked me if I would bring together the statements which have been made on behalf of the corporation in connection with the matter which has been occupying the press over the last few days. 66968-9-330

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Very well. This is the statement issued by Mr. Bushnell to the press on Monday, June 22, as I am advised:
Some two weeks ago the corporation decided to replace the "Preview Commentary" from Ottawa, which followed the eight o'clock C.B.C. news, with a "Special Parliamentary Report" prepared by the C.B.C. news service. It was felt that this would improve the corporation's service of reporting the proceedings of the previous day in parliament.
This has been followed by resignations of several members of the corporation's talks and public affairs national office in Toronto, on the grounds that the substitution of the opinion broadcast "Preview Commentary" by the factual C.B.C. news report implied political interference with the C.B.C.'s broadcasting of controversial affairs. The corporation does not accept this implication.
The C.B.C. has the fullest confidence in the talks and public affairs department which over the years has contributed some of the C.B.C.'s most distinguished and responsible broadcasting.
Then I am advised that on June 24, following a series of meetings of the board of directors which had taken place in Toronto, the following statement was made at six o'clock in the evening:
Since the C.B.C. board of directors began its regular meetings in Toronto, assertions have been made that a directive of management which replaced the "Preview Commentary" by a factual report on the daily proceedings in parliament was prompted by considerations incompatible with the independence of the C.B.C. The board and management of the corporation are convinced that the intent of the directive has been misinterpreted by the public. Accordingly, and in order to remove any doubt as to the independence of the corporation, "Preview Commentary" will be resumed on Monday of next week.
The board of directors and management of C.B.C. at this time wish to reaffirm the established policy of freedom of expression in C.B.C. programs devoted to the discussion of public issues.
Following that Mr. Walker, of Toronto, issued this statement on June 24:
Mr. H. G. Walker, the director for Ontario and English networks division of the C.B.C., announced tonight that the resignations submitted by employees earlier this week have not been accepted by C.B.C. management. Mr. Walker hopes that all employees will find it possible to resume their normal duties.
And in connection with resignations, I am advised that none of the resignations have been accepted by the corporation and that all the employees have returned to work except Mr. Peers, supervisor of talks and public affairs, Mr. Hugh Gillis, his assistant and Mr. Bernard Trotter, who have said they did not want any action taken on their resignations until they have appeared before the House of Commons committee on broadcasting tomorrow.



That comprises the official record of the documents. I am told that Mr. Bushnell held a press conference, but I have not seen any notes of this and I believe no record was kept, except what subsequently appeared in the press, and I also understand that Mr. Bushnell made a statement over the C.B.C. in an interview, notes of which I have not in my possession.
While I am on my feet, so that the record may be complete, may I refer to the series of questions which the Leader of the Opposition asked me last week when I was away. I think perhaps these questions should be answered here now so as to make a continuous record. The Leader of the Opposition asked, as recorded on page 5086 of Hansard:
Were discussions held in the past ten days in Toronto or Ottawa between management of the C.B.C. and persons who have since resigned from their posts in the corporation?
The answer is yes.
I was also asked:
If so, who were present at these discussions for C.B.C. management and for talks and public affairs personnel.
The answer is, Mr. E. L. Bushnell for management and Mr. Frank Peers for the talks and public affairs department. The last part of the question was:
How many such meetings were held, and on what dates?
The answer is that one meeting was held, on Sunday, June 21. That is the full answer to the questions asked by the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Essex East also asked questions with respect to the resignations, but as I have already stated all the persons concerned except the three I have named have returned to work, and I am not in a position to give more detailed answers to those questions than those I have just given.
When I referred to this matter on Thursday morning, I think it was, when I returned from St. Catharines, I said I would make a statement to the House on Monday. I think that was an unfortunate phrase. I was not thinking at that time that these gentlemen were appearing before the committee or that this was a continuing matter, and I think it would be improper for me, as this matter is sub judice, to comment on the broader implications of this matter until the committee has considered whatever evidence may be brought before it and taken whatever action it may wish to take as far as examining witnesses is concerned. For that reason I do not propose to say anything on that particular issue until it has been clarified and dealt with by our committee of the House of Commons.
[Mr. Nowlan.l
However, with the permission of the house I would like to say a word about Mr. Bushnell, whose name has appeared in the press in the last few days in various reports and rumours of impending resignations and so on. Mr. Bushnell was appointed assistant general manager of this corporation when it was reorganized last fall. Mr. Ouimet was made general manager. Mr. Ouimet was appointed president and Mr. Bushnell vicepresident respectively.
In December the corporation was faced with the strike of Radio Canada. Mr. Ouimet had been away. He returned and tried to deal with that strike. As a result he collapsed, and as we all know has been seriously ill since that time. I am glad to say that his doctors report that they think he can return to work within a matter of two or three weeks, although not to assume full responsibility initially. As a result of that illness Mr. Bushnell carried on not only as assistant general manager but as general manager, as president and vice-president. In other words, he was doing the work of two men.
Those of us in this house who have been close to the situation in the last few months -and I see this was mentioned in the Canadian Press dispatch in this morning's papers-are aware that the last six months have been probably the most hectic in the history of the corporation. I can say of my personal knowledge that during this period Mr. Bushnell has worked tirelessly and given himself wholeheartedly and solely to the corporation. I know that on many occasions he worked 17 or 18 hours a day throughout the strike. Although I am not a doctor I can tell hon. members-and I have had advice to this effect as well-that Mr. Bushnell is completely and totally exhausted after having carried this heavy burden during this period of time. In fact I have been afraid that we would have more than one man in hospital with a heart attack and I still fear this possibility.
Mr. Bushnell is carrying on and intends to carry on despite reports to the contrary. There has never been any thought of his not being here until this committee has finished its investigation into this particular phase in the matter of interference with the corporation. I hope when this has been concluded Mr. Bushnell will be able to get away for a few weeks rest-and I say "few weeks" advisedly-because I am told that the answers concerning other matters to be examined into by the committee can be supplied by other officials of the corporation, and it will not be necessary for Mr. Bushnell to be present.

Mr. Bushnell inherited the situation and did not create it. He was recommended to me by the former general manager and chairman of the board and by all the senior officials of the corporation, I was told, I believed, and I still believe that the morale of the corporation might have been prejudiced if Mr. Bushnell and Mr. Ouimet had not been appointed as president and vice president.
During the last few days I have personally received many telephone calls from officers and employees of the corporation not only from Ottawa but elsewhere across the country telling me of their confidence in Mr. Bushnell and their resentment at the charges of weakness and incompetence and so on and so forth which have been made against him.
I can only say that I have been closely associated with him, as I was with Mr. Ouimet prior to his illness, since the day they became president and vice president of the corporation. I must say I have heard from Mr. Bushnell some "Bushnellisms" because our discussions have been frank and free in dealing with all aspects of the corporation. I have seen no sign of weakness or incompetence. I personally believe that Mr. Bushnell deserves the confidence of the country and the corporation for the way he has given to it of his strength and his whole being during these very difficult months.

Children's Diseases Research Fund given to the several readings to the end, it it meets with the approval of the house, that the legislation might be passed today and be made available for consideration in the other place.
I would point out first that it was on June 11 that the decision of the government of Canada was announced that in place of the usual gifts that are made to Her Majesty on great state occasions such as a visitation by her, it was decided that course should not be followed and that Canadians as a whole would like to see something of a memorial of the visit which would be generally beneficial to Her Majesty's subjects in Canada. As reported at page 4559 of Hansard I set forth the proposal which is now represented by the bill before the house.
In the course of the discussion the Leader of the Opposition mentioned a matter that had already received the consideration of the government. He suggested that with respect to the fund to be set up, provision might be made to enable private citizens to make contributions. I would ask leave of the house to make some reference to the several sections of the bill, though normally this is not done on second reading. I should like to answer by way of anticipation the questions that I believe might arise. The first would naturally be the wording of the preamble. The preamble is somewhat different from the normal preamble in that it starts with these words:
Most Gracious Sovereign,
Whereas it has pleased Your Majesty to approve the suggestion that the occasion of your visit to Canada and your personal interest in the wellbeing of children should be marked by the establishment in your name of a fund to be devoted to the furthering of research into the diseases of children and the prevention and cure of such diseases, to which all who wish in this way to make a gift to Your Majesty may contribute-
The wording is somewhat similar to the wording of appropriation bills. Then follows the actual enacting section:
May it therefore please Your Majesty, that it may be enacted-
And so on. The purpose is to set up a fund to be known as the Queen Elizabeth II Canadian research fund to aid in research into the diseases of children. This is an objective that through the years has represented a particular interest on the part of Her Majesty. Her interest in children has been pre-eminent. On the occasion of her present visit one is more impressed than ever with the fact that while she occupies the position of Queen of Canada and in other parts of the commonwealth that of Queen of the several dominions and in still others that of head of the


commonwealth, her interest in children is apparent wherever she appears.
As I said a moment ago, this fund has been generally applauded and approved throughout the country. Indeed, it has been most interesting during the past few weeks to have noted that several provinces-such as the province of Ontario and the province of Alberta-have set up funds for educational purposes and the provision of scholarships, those matters being within the exclusive ambit and jurisdiction of provincial authority. In the province of Quebec a fund has been set up for heart disease research. In other words, this visit in general will be marked by provision being made in many parts of our country for beneficial steps to raise standards both of education and health, to the end that Her Majesty's subjects may enjoy ever increasing standards.
In no field has it been more apparent that action should be taken than in the field of children's diseases. Indeed, the tremendous changes which have taken place in the last 25 or 50 years in this and other fields have brought about an increase in life expectancy. There are those who today predict that in consequence of medical advance in research within this century, a man may well look forward, where the highest medical standards prevail, to an expectancy of close to 100 years.
In order to make this fund widely available for support on the part of Canadians as a whole and also of individuals who choose to make contributions, provision is made that gifts, bequests, appropriations and other contributions may be made not only now but throughout the years that follow while this fund is being administered. In the typewritten draft which was delivered to the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia, section 5, subsection 2 provided that a chairman and six trustees be appointed by Her Majesty the Queen by commission under the great seal of Canada. The law officers have advised me today that there is no necessity to have that section included, and all contributions made will be subject to the usual rules respecting contributions to charitable organizations under the Income Tax Act. Therefore there will be no need to have that portion of section 5 included in the bill.
In so far as the purposes are concerned, those purposes are set forth in section 3. That section provides that the fund is to assist individuals or organizations to carry on research into the diseases of children and the causes, prevention and treatment of such diseases. There is also provision for an audit

and a report to parliament so that parliament, having contributed on behalf of the Canadian people $1 million, will exercise that degree of parliamentary control which is essential in expenditures made by parliament and on behalf of the Canadian people.
I think there is nothing further that I need add. The general acceptance of the principle was made clear by members representing the official opposition and the C.C.F. group when the matter first came before the house. I believe this is a major step forward in achieving that relationship between the Queen and her subjects which represents something mystical and yet real, which was so apparent two days ago at the opening of the St. Lawrence waterway when she represented the people of Canada, and in co-operation with the President of the United States gave an exemplification of cooperation which might well be the hope of other parts of the world. In her person she represents the unity of our nation within the commonwealth, and in the personification of her position through funds such as this she typifies the essence of democracy, which is co-operation for the benefit of all her subjects.

Mr. Speaker, it is not of course, normal procedure to put a bill through all stages, as we are doing today with this bill, in such a short period of time before, indeed, we have had an opportunity in advance to study the bill. But, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, the circumstances are not normal. Even in respect of the language of the bill we are impressed by the fact that the circumstances are not normal. Not only are they abnormal; they are very happy indeed, and are circumstances which make it desirable to put this bill through the house in one day so it can be passed by the time the Queen reaches her capital tomorrow.
The objective of the bill, Mr. Speaker, is one which will appeal, I am sure, to all Canadians, designed as it is to facilitate research into children's diseases; and we are sure that objective will be aided by this particular act. We know the need. We know also there is great need of research in other related fields, such as heart disease and cancer. This particular bill will make a contribution to this need. I am glad the Prime Minister and the government have seen fit to include in the bill a provision by which individuals may make contributions to the fund. It will associate individuals with the government in pursuit of a worthy objective.
Mr. Speaker, I am reminded that in the celebration of King George V's jubilee some years ago a fund was set up for cancer research to which contributions came from

Children's Diseases Research Fund individual Canadians to an amount, I think, of something over half a million dollars. It was a fund which did much at that time to facilitate research into this dread disease, as also I am sure this fund will do at this time. I recall that that particular fund was put under the trusteeship of the prime minister, the chief justice, and I think also the leader of the opposition, and I believe it was an effectively administered fund, as I know this will be. speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-57, an act respecting the superannuation of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-Mr. Fulton-Mr. Sevigny in the chair.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance explained that the purpose of this bill was to revise the old Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act and make it less confusing, but after reading this bill I have reached the conclusion that far from being less confusing it is more confusing and incomprehensible. It would have been better to change the former act and leave just one piece of legislation on the statute books instead of creating several acts referring one to the other. For instance, the former act used to bear the name Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act which is precisely the short title of Bill C-34. The former act has been amended and bears the name Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act. It was formerly chapter 241 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1953.
An examination of the new bill indicates that most sections of the former act have been repealed with the exception of four or five sections. While the former act is repealed we see that the new bill makes many references to the former act, which still applies to some members of the force who get benefits under the new bill. It is difficult to understand how we can determine what section of the act will apply to one particular member of the force if we have to consult anywhere from three to six acts in order to learn what a member is entitled to. The new bill refers many times to the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian forces superannuation act and the former act which has been repealed. The minister has made the law much more confused than it was previously.
Another criticism of the new bill arises from the fact that interpretations or definitions of words are scattered throughout the bill. Clause 2 gives definitions of a few words, but others are defined in other clauses. Clause 6 subclause 2 defines "interests", clause 8 subclause 1 defines "annuity", "immediate annuity", "deferred annuity", "cash termination allowance" and "return of contributions". Clause 14 defines "widow" and "widower", clause 15 defines "recipient", clause 17 defines "elective contributor" and clause 29 defines "former act". Does the minister not agree that there should be one definition clause or interpretation section?
66968-9-331
R.C.M.P. Act
Another weakness of the new bill is that some clauses contain sentences ranging from 37 to 42 lines in length without a period. Clause 5 contains a sentence of over 104 lines. When you reach the end of it and encounter the verb you have forgotten the subject to which it applies. I know it will be answered that these are excerpts from old acts, but my main criticism is that instead of one comprehensive act we now have five or more.
Bill No. C-57 is called the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act. We have also recently passed Bill No. C-34, which bears the name Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. This was the name of the former act now amended by Bill No. C-57, which will hereafter be referred to as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act. Sometimes the bill refers to the former act which applies to some members of the force. Therefore reference is made to a former act which has been repealed. I understand that the word "repealed" means the act is no longer in effect. When the next revised statutes of Canada are printed I am sure they will not contain former acts which have been repealed, and in order to get information in respect to certain cases we will have to refer back to previous revised statutes in orders to obtain the information we seek.
Surely it would have been less confusing if we could have had one act to cover every circumstance and case. I have observed that words such as "pension" "benefit" and "contribution" are interpreted in the same way and repeated in all these bills or acts. The Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act are based on the same principle, so there could be one piece of legislation dealing with all the categories of people mentioned who take advantage of these various clauses. My good friend will deal with this in more detail when we come to the different sections.
I regret that the Minister of Justice, in introducing new bills to clarify the matter or make it less confusing, has missed the point. I ask him to see next year or two years from now whether he cannot take advantage of these suggestions and instead of having four, five or six bills which are intermingled, introduce one clear bill which will apply to every category of the R.C.M. Police, the Canadian forces and the civil service. If he will look into all the acts covering these people he will find that the ways of calculating the service one has given to the government come to about the same thing. Sometimes there may be a difference of one or

R.C.M.P. Act
two years, as we said when we discussed Bill No. C-37. Sometimes one category has a greater advantage than the other but still some of these bills are much more confused than they were before.
It is very difficult to interpret this new bill which refers to the former act, which is being repealed in respect of some of its contents but still bears another name. I ask the Minister of Justice and his officials to introduce a new superannuation bill next year so that anyone who wishes to look into it in order to find his own category will not have to refer to four or five other acts, or to a law which is repealed except for a few sections.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise at this point a question which I was not aware of when the Canadian forces superannuation act was discussed either in principle on second reading or in committee of the whole. I was informed that there is some difference with respect to the Canadian forces, the civil service and the R.C.M.P. retirement leave or rehabilitation leave. A member of the Canadian army or of the Canadian navy with 20 years' service is granted before retirement four months' rehabilitation leave plus 30 days annual leave. I am told that is done according to the regulations of those services. In the civil service a man with 20 years' service is granted three months' rehabilitation leave plus one month annual leave, as he is entitled to under the regulations.
I am told that in the R.C.M.P. it is quite different. A man with 20 years' service actually is granted two months' rehabilitation leave and in some cases is granted annual leave only because I am told, the annual leave in the R.C.M.P. cannot be taken unless the person actually worked in that particular fiscal year. Therefore it would seem to me there is a difference of appreciation of service of some kind, or a difference in the chance that a member of either of those forces has as opposed to those in civil life.
As I said before, retirement leave is known in all the services. The Canadian forces, the civil service and the R.C.M.P. have rehabilitation leave. This is given on the grounds that those persons are subject to transfer during the last period of service, and to provide those persons with a chance to decide where they will establish their domicile at retirement on pension. It may be that a person who enlisted in the R.C.M.P. while he was domiciled in Nova Scotia may reach the retirement stage of his career in Alberta. This leave is given to him in order to give him a chance, as I said, to decide where to go on retirement.

As I said earlier, in the civil service an individual receives three months' rehabilitation leave, and in the Canadian forces he receives four months. Why is it not possible for all these public servants, the Canadian forces personnel, the R.C.M.P. personnel, to be given the same period of rehabilitation or retirement leave?
This is a point I was not aware of earlier. If I had been I would have raised it on the bill presented by the Minister of National Defence. I want to raise it now so the Minister of Justice will be able to consult with the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State to try to iron out those differences and give the R.C.M.P. personnel the same chance that the members of the Canadian forces have, and so that at the same time the members of the public service will have the same chance as the Canadian forces personnel, namely the four months' rehabilitation leave and the 30 days annual leave.
I raise this point now because I was unable to see where in the act I could raise it.

Mr. Chairman, to deal first with the point raised by the hon. member for Megantic, I should explain that retirement leave does not form part of the provisions regarding superannuation. It is, therefore, not covered in any way in the superannuation bill. Retirement leave in the police is taken care of by the regulations under the main act which we recently passed in this house.
I am informed that with respect to both the armed forces and the public service generally the same scheme is followed, that the question of retirement leave is covered by regulations under the National Defence Act or under the Civil Service Act, as the case may be. So in no case are the provisions for retirement leave set or even regulated under the superannuation act. They are covered by regulations under the main acts in each case.
It is true that there are variations in the amounts of retirement leave made available as between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other branches of the public service, but we have prepared and have ready now for submission to treasury board new draft regulations under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act when it shall have become law, and those regulations will introduce uniform standards, in so far as uniform standards are possible, as between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and other branches of the public service.

speechtext:
Treasury board staff, treasury board officials-and in that way there is assurance that they will be co-ordinated and in so far as possible differences as between various branches of the public service will be eliminated.
With respect to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Denis, I have to confess that the R.C.M.P. superannuation bill is a complicated measure. It may not be a completely adequate defence but I can defend it in part at least on the ground that that is true of other superannuation measures, the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Canadian forces superannuation bill which was approved by the house just recently. But I can assure him that, again in so far as it is possible to do so, the three measures will now proceed on exactly the same basis and there will be uniformity in the superannuation provisions applicable to the public service generally, the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of Canada. This bill then is of a uniform pattern with the other superannuation measures passed by parliament.
I also agree with him that it is perhaps unfortunate that there must be a reference back to other measures, but unless we made reference back to other measures under which pensions have been payable to members of the force in the past I can assure my hon. friend that this bill, as my officials suggest, might be at least twice as complicated as it is at the moment and certainly would be twice as long.
I am interested in the suggestion that there should be one general superannuation act covering all branches of the public service, that is, the civil service, the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. I would have thought it more efficient and clearer to have three separate bills, because inevitably there are certain differences in the conditions of service and thus in the superannuation benefits as between the three services. I would think that if you had one general act you would have to introduce so many detailed provisions making variations and exceptions that you would not in fact accomplish the object of clarity.
It is a matter in which other ministers are just as concerned as I am; therefore it is

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we were considering the previous measure having to do with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police I asked the minister a question and made some reference to the superannuation for the retiring commissioner. At that time the minister pointed out to me that the appropriate time to deal with that matter would be when the measure now before us came up for consideration. I am having a little difficulty in trying to locate the clause which might deal with that phase of superannuation. May I also say to the minister that I hold no brief from the retiring commissioner to speak about the matter, but my interest is more than just academic. My interest stems

R.C.M.P. Act
from the fact that a very formidable editorial appeared in the Montreal Star which raised the question, and it is quite possible that similar situations might arise in the future.
I do not have to discuss at this time the merits of the retiring commissioner, and I know the minister has recognized the great service he has rendered to the country. But there seems to be a feeling, as expressed in the Montreal Star, that here is a man who retired almost at the point when he would have reached his maximum superannuation, and he did not retire for any of the causes mentioned in the act which would in some way disqualify him. I am raising this point now on clause 1 because I do not know on what clause I can discuss the matter. I do not know whether it would be clause 17 dealing with special cases, clause 20 dealing with the establishment of a pension board or clause 21 which sets up regulations for the pension board.
I am hopeful that somewhere within these sections there is a provision that could enable the pension board or parliament or the governor in council to say, or would give them the authority to say, either dealing with this case or any similar case in the future, that here is a public servant who has given Canada very satisfactory and excellent service but who through circumstances of a disagreement felt it was not consistent to hold his job-whatever the circumstances, he retires; and he retires, I do not say with the blessing of the minister or of the house but certainly without any hostility-and it is felt that after 20 some years of service he should not be prejudiced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Thirty-four years.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister says 34 years. That makes my case still stronger. I am not arguing Mr. Nicholson's case. I am arguing the case generally of a man who has had that record and who has actually been prejudiced by his retirement through no fault of his own, and am asking whether a provision should not be created, if one does not exist, by which the country can say to a man like that, "You are on the point of retiring; you have another year or two years to go. We will grant you two years' leave of absence and allow you to retire on your full pension". I believe it would be a popular measure throughout the country, and I believe it would be well received.
While we cannot decorate a man for public service of this kind, we can recognize it to some extent by seeing that he is not prejudiced. I do not care what the amount involved is. He should be permitted to retire on full pension and a fortiori if he has only one more year to go in order to achieve it.

What provision is there in the act that would enable parliament, the pension board or the governor in council to deal with a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is no provision in the act or in the bill before us which would enable parliament or the governor in council to deal, of its own motion as it were under the act, with a case of that kind. A special case of the type which this retirement certainly represents would, in my opinion, not be a proper one to cover in an act of general application.
The scheme of a retirement or superannuation act such as this one or the old parts of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act which it replaces is, especially in the case of officers, to require a period of minimum service which must be fulfilled before full pension will be payable to an officer who retires voluntarily. I think this is a sound provision because, it will be appreciated, the organization of the force would be difficult to maintain if there were any encouragement or, indeed, if there were any lack of discouragement of officers, particularly those in key positions, retiring before they have served the length of time which it is agreed it is reasonable to ask for.
Second, there is a substantial investment__
to put the matter on economic terms alone_____
in the training and careers of officers and it is therefore a matter of policy to discourage them from retiring voluntarily before they have completed the minimum length of service. In the case of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the minimum length of service for officers is 35 years. That is the minimum length of service before full pension will be paid on voluntary retirement. After he has completed 35 years of service an officer may retire voluntarily and he will get the full pension which he has earned by his length of service. But in order to carry out the policy to which I have referred, namely to discourage voluntary retirement while an officer is still able to serve efficiently, there is in the present act, in section 45, a provision that an officer who retires voluntarily after 25 years of service but with less than 35 years of service is entitled to a pension for life of 20 per cent less than he would have been entitled to if he were retired compulsorily.
That provision is in there for this purpose. As will be appreciated, if an officer is retired compulsorily before he completes his full term of service-either because, let us say, he incurs some medical or physical disability which makes him unable efficiently to serve or if for any other reason it becomes desirable to discharge him from the force or to remove

him from the force-it should be possible to retire him compulsorily without his incurring any penalty with respect to his pension. That is why the section to which I have referred, namely section 45, is framed in that way; that an officer retiring voluntarily after 25 years' service is entitled to a pension for life 20 per cent less than he would be entitled to if he were retired compulsorily. But the effect of that provision-and it is a principle with which I agree-is to deprive an officer who retires voluntarily before he has completed the full length of service of a portion of his pension. It is a penalty with respect to which the act leaves no option. As I have said, I think it is a sound position for the reasons I have given.
With respect to the individual case of Commissioner Nicholson, however, I am reasonably convinced that parliament did not intend that type of case to be covered or be dealt with in this way, or that parliament would not have intended that case to be dealt with in this way if it had been before parliament at the time the act was being drafted. Here you have a case, as the hon. gentleman says, of an officer within one year or, I think it was, one year and some three days, of the maximum length of service, namely 35 years, after which he would have been able to retire voluntarily on full pension and who felt in his conscience that he was unable to continue to serve for reasons which were given and which we do not need to go into here. He therefore felt called upon to retire.
This is not the ordinary case of an officer just deciding after a certain period, "I want to get out. I can go out on full pension and therefore I will go." This was an exceptional case. I do not know that there has ever been a case like this one previously. However, as I have said, the act left no option but to impose -if I may put it that way-a 20 per cent penalty. As I have already said, I am quite certain that parliament would not have intended this particular case to be dealt with in this way. However, I was and I am still unable to deal with it in any other way in view of the provisions of the act as enacted by parliament. I do not think we should change the provision of the new bill to provide exceptions of general application, because I think cases such as this are so exceptional that it would be unsound to introduce them into the bill.
However, what I should like to say is that I have been concerned over the fact that the former commissioner, following what he regarded to be an honourable course, a course which he felt he had no option but to follow, should have been penalized in this way. While, as I say, I had some disagreement with him as to whether he was right in following that
R.C.M.P. Act
course, and I made it clear that I did not think he was right, nevertheless I respected his motives and his sincerity. However, only parliament can adjust the situation. My hands and those of the governor in council are tied by the provision of the pension act.
In order to bring this matter to a head I am prepared to say this. If there is any indication from parliament, as constituted here in committee of the whole of the House of Commons, that they agree with what my hon. friend opposite has said and with what I have just said as to the undesirability of penalizing an officer with this record, and if I have any general indication that parliament would like to see the matter rectified or ad-adjusted in this individual case, I would be perfectly prepared and indeed happy to recommend to my colleagues that an appropriate provision be inserted in the estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for next year. It would be a provision having legislative effect. It would be a provision the effect of which would be to restore to this particular person the pension he would have got had he completed his full 35 years of service.

On clause 10, I do not remember if the Minister of Justice was in this committee on June 23 when I raised a question with the Minister of National Defence on the other bill. I would refer the minister to page 5046 of Hansard of June 23. I would not like to repeat the entire argument I made then, but I should like to summarize, otherwise I would not be logical with myself. I am taking the clause as a whole. Under 10(1), a member who has less than 10 years' service is entitled to a return of contributions or to a cash termination allowance, or if he has served in the forces for 10 or more years he is entitled to an annuity. Under subclause 2, that is the case of a member retiring on account of a disability after less than 10 years, he is entitled to a return of contributions or a cash allowance, but if he has 10 or more years' service he is entitled to an annuity. It seems to me that these two subsections referring to a member who has reached the retirement age or to a member who is disabled are alike, and that the member is entitled to exactly the same benefit.
However subclause 3 provides an immediate annuity after more than 20 years' service. It seems to me there is a certain degree of discrimination there. If a man is retired before reaching retirement age he is entitled to benefits. If he is disabled he is entitled to exactly the same. If he is retired from the force for reasons of economy or efficiency it is not his fault, and it seems to me that he is penalized. If he reaches retirement age it is not the fault of the force. Under subclause 3 he seems to have less choice or option than other members under subclauses 1 and 2.
I have prepared an informal amendment to subclause 3. I am afraid that if I move it I will be declared out of order because perhaps it would add a burden to the treasury. I should like to read the amendment

as I have prepared it and submit it to the minister for his consideration. Perhaps he will get in touch with the Minister of National Defence, who has the same problem, and then ask the members of the other place to study the amendment and perhaps move it in the other place.
My proposed informal amendment reads:
That subclause 3 of clause 10 be amended by deleting subparagraphs (a), (b) and (c) thereof and by substituting therefor the following subparagraphs :
(a)	If he has served in the force for less than ten years, he is entitled to
(i)	a return of contributions, or
(ii)	a cash termination alowance, whichever is the greater, and
(b)	If he has served in the force for ten or more years, he is entitled to an immediate annuity.
As I say, I am not moving this as a formal amendment because it would be out of order coming from a member of the opposition rather than a member of the government. However, I should like to submit it to the minister so he could consider it in the meantime before the bill goes to the other place. On the other hand, if he wishes to consider it now I should be happy to have him do so.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate
the care with which the hon. gentleman has studied this matter and prepared his suggested amendment, but without making a final decision as to whether or not I could accept it at the moment I must say to the hon. gentleman that it does run counter to the principle upon which clause 10 has been prepared. That principle very definitely is to treat more generously those who are retired by reason of disability than those who are retired compulsorily for any other reason such as to promote efficiency or economy. We feel that those who have to retire because they have incurred some disability while they have been serving members are entitled to more generous treatment than those who have to be retired without having incurred disability for such reasons as to promote economy or efficiency, because in the former case the member would have continued to be a useful and valuable member of the force but he has been disabled through no fault of his own. In the latter case the member would not continue to be a useful and valuable member of the force and that is why he is retired compulsorily.
It has been felt as a matter of general principle that the former member should be treated more generously than the latter. I would not care to be taken as giving any commitment that we would depart from that principle, but I will study the proposed amendment. If I can see my way clear to accepting it I shall do so, but it must be understood that I am not to be taken now

to be giving a commitment to accept it. If that is understood I am prepared to leave it there.

The purpose of this bill is to revise the Seeds Act to meet recent trends and developments In the production, processing and merchandising of seeds. The bill contemplates no substantive changes in policy and is in a form similar to other agricultural statutes enacted in recent years.
The Seeds Act is the instrument which ensures the reliability of seeds sold to Canadian farmers. The first legislation in this field was introduced in 1905 and the present act has been on the statute books since 1923, which is the reason that a revision is necessary at this time.
The act and the regulations under it establish quality standards for seeds for such factors as germination and purity; require imported seed to meet minimum quality standards; and provide for the licensing of new varieties of certain crops and for the grading of registered seed produced under crop pedigree certificates of the Canadian Seed

Seeds Act
Growers' Association. It is in connection with this act that seed testing laboratories are maintained by the department.
The bill to revise the act in no way changes the basic requirements of the present statute. The act now, however, contains certain provisions of detail of a nature which require amendment from time to time to conform to changing conditions of seed production and distribution. These have to do with such matters as markings on seed containers, the specific grades which are to be used for seeds, the types of inspection certificates which are to be issued, and the crops to which variety licensing is to apply. Several of these detailed provisions are in need of revision, and representations to that effect have been made by the Canadian Seed Growers' Association and the Canadian Seed Trade Association, the two bodies chiefly concerned with this act and regulations under it.
These detailed requirements are deleted from the bill revising the act and authority is provided to prescribe them by regulation of the governor in council. The bill in this respect is in a form similar to other agricultural statutes enacted in recent years.
I might mention one matter which will be familiar to any hon. members associated with seed production and which constituted one reason for revising the act. The act now establishes two classes of pedigreed seed, namely registered and certified. Registered seed is based on the registration of crops by the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, while certified seed is based on the certification of crops by the department. These two services are, under present conditions, a duplication of each other, since both serve the purpose of guaranteeing the purchaser seed which is of a pure variety. The seed growers' association and other agricultural interests have urged that this duplication be removed.
The bill to revise the act, unlike the present act, does not establish classes and grades for seeds directly. It requires that seed must conform to prescribed standards and provides for grades to be established by regulation and for the use of the standards of the Canadian Seed Growers' Association. The present duplication between registered and certified seed can therefore be removed in the grades to be established by regulation under the act, and crop registration by the Canadian Seed Growers' Association can be recognized for grades of pedigreed seed.
I am pleased to be able to inform the house that the bill was approved both by the Canadian Seed Growers' Association and the Canadian Seed Trade Association at their recent annual convention in western Canada.

The main change involved-

Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this legislation does something to stir my memories of years ago. We have come a long way in the past 25 or 30 years with respect to the registration and certification of seed. A classmate of mine at the Ontario Agricultural College, who graduated in 1913, went to British Columbia and became an official of the Department of Agriculture. It was his responsibility, under the Conservative government of the day, to visit the various farms on which seed was grown and to inspect potato crops for certification. On one occasion he went to the farm of a very prominent grower on Vancouver island who had, I think, 20 acres of potatoes which he wished to have inspected as certified seed
Seeds Act
potatoes, and he refused to do so because the crop had a certain percentage of mosaic.
He reported to the deputy minister of agriculture, who was quite concerned and said, "Now, look here; do you not realize that this man is a very influential Conservative on Vancouver island, and that it makes a very great difference to him so far as price is concerned whether or not this seed is certified? I suggest that you go back and have another look." So he went back and had another look to make certain, but he did not change his mind. He came back again and turned in a similar report. The result of the faithfulness, shall I say, of that civil servant to the law and to the high standards that were set was that he was promptly discharged. Later he went to work as senior agriculturist for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
I am not saying that this practice, which was quite prevalent in those days, was peculiar to one party more than the other, but I know from personal experience that there were certain political overtones with regard to the inspection of crops or seeds for registration or certification.
As I said before, we have come a long way since then, and I am very glad to know that the government has introduced this bill after receiving representations from the Canadian Seed Growers' Association and the Canadian Seed Trade Association, and that both these associations have endorsed the terms of the legislation. Why has there been this great improvement? I think, using the words of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, it is because of the influence of farm organizations, seed growers associations and the seed trade association.
