subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the payment of contributions and the making of loans by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund, in respect of the operation of provincial schemes for crop insurance.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. McCleave in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose at this stage to speak rather briefly on the crop insurance proposal, and I shall go into the matter in considerably more detail on second reading, at which time copies of the bill will be in the hands of hon. members and they will thus be in a better position to understand completely what I am talking about.
The demand for all-risk crop insurance, as I am sure all hon. members of the committee are aware, has been quite strong for many
Crop Insurance
years. There has been a great deal of talk about an all-risk crop insurance scheme being put into effect. Many bodies of various kinds and many individuals have examined into the matter both here and in other countries, and various schemes have been put into operation in other countries including the United States.
During the past two years during which I have been in charge of the Department of Agriculture, officials of the department have been studying and assessing the schemes in operation, particularly those in operation immediately to the south of us in the western United States. The officials have also studied the reports which have been made by Canadian commissions, boards, individuals and others who have studied crop insurance and made recommendations in connection therewith. There is a considerable mass of material in connection with this matter. Unfortunately, however, when one comes to examine it there are very few what you might call definite recommendations which have been made by the various bodies that have investigated crop insurance.
I should like to point out that our constitutional set-up places property and civil rights under the provinces and that this would constitute a bar to a wholly federal crop insurance scheme. Of course that problem might be overcome by getting the consent of the provinces to such a scheme. However, without that consent-and we have no means of knowing whether or not it could be obtained-a wholly federal crop insurance scheme could not be put into operation. In addition, the studies carried on in connection with crop insurance indicate that conditions vary so greatly from province to province that a scheme which would work well and be practical in one province would not work at all in another province.
We have come to the conclusion that the only practical means of dealing with crop insurance is to employ the same principle that has been used in making construction grants for hospitals and in the hospital insurance scheme. In other words, it would be necessary for the dominion government to lay down certain minimum requirements. If these minimum requirements were met by a scheme set up by the provincial authorities the federal government could then make certain grants and loans.
I shall briefly outline what these grants and loans are proposed to be. The crop insurance bill which will be brought in following this resolution will authorize the Minister of Agriculture, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into agreements with the provinces to provide for the payment by Canada to the provinces in respect

Crop Insurance
of costs incurred by the provinces in the operation of crop insurance schemes. It will also provide for making loans to provinces for the operation of such insurance schemes. The contributions and loans are:
(1)	Payment by Canada of 50 per cent of the administration costs of any scheme set up by a province.
(2)	Payment by Canada of 20 per cent of the premiums charged.
(3)	Loans to provinces in the amount of 75 per cent of the amount required to meet indemnity commitments less $200,000. In other words, if the indemnity commitment-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Would you mind repeating that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
I will repeat it in this way. If the indemnity commitment in the first year that the insurance scheme was in operation was greater than the amount of the premiums which had been collected-which could very readily be the case, as the hon. member who is familiar with insurance matters knows-then, if that shortage in the insurance fund was not more than $200,000 the province would not be entitled to a loan, because it was considered that any province is in a position without endangering its financial situation to meet demands of $200,000. But if the shortage is in excess of $200,000, then the province is entitled to secure a loan from the dominion government up to 75 per cent of the amount of the shortage. The purpose of this provision is to place provinces in the situation where, if they happen to meet a very bad crop year, particularly in the first two years of operation of the scheme before the fund had been built up, they would not be financially embarrassed as a result.
One of the chief objections which has been raised in some of the provinces to a crop insurance scheme is this very matter, that if they did meet a bad year, or particularly two bad years, in the early years in which the scheme was in operation it would cripple the provinces financially and make their entire financing very difficult if not impossible. That is the reason for this loan provision.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Would that be $200,000 for each province?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: You said "for a province".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
The scheme which is entered into with each province really would be a separate scheme. We will make an agreement with each province in regard to the scheme of insurance which they set up and if they have a loss which is more than $200,000 more than the amount that they have in the kitty,

we will say, then they are entitled to secure a loan of 75 per cent of that amount from the dominion government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: That is for each province?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Yes, certainly.
The financial assistance which it is proposed to provide will be available on condition that the crop insurance schemes are actuarially sound. In other words, this is designed to be an insurance scheme and not any type of what you might call a relief scheme such as we have had under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Many people have looked upon prairie farm assistance as an insurance scheme. It was distinctly stated at the time it was brought in that it was not an insurance scheme and that point has been made constantly ever since. It was really a drought relief scheme and it continues basically to be that. This scheme is to set up an actual insurance scheme and one which will be actuarially sound but one to which of course the dominion government will assist in the cost and financing through paying 50 per cent of the administration costs and 20 per cent of the premium costs.
I was saying that this assistance will be available on condition that the crop insurance scheme is actuarially sound; that is, that it is a scheme which on statistical information or evidence would mean that sufficient money would be collected over a long period of years to pay the indemnities which would have to be met; and next, that a minimum number or proportion of farmers come into the scheme. In other words, you cannot put in an insurance scheme in which you take in only the very poor risks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: There is no compulsion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
No; so far as our proposal is concerned there is no compulsion. The purpose here is to make this scheme as flexible as possible so that each province will be in as favourable a position as possible to set up a scheme which will be adapted to its own conditions. Owing to the fact that I mentioned earlier, namely that conditions do vary so much in Canada, it is impossible to lay down hard and fast conditions covering every crop which is grown in every part of Canada. Therefore, you must leave it up to the provinces to determine what crops they wish to cover and what the contributions are going to be in connection with those particular crops.
But as far as we are concerned, we will not pay the grant to the provinces unless, as I said, first, it is an actuarially sound scheme; and, second, that the minimum number or

proportionate number of farmers come under the scheme. What we have in mind at the present time is 25 per cent of the farmers or of the acreage in whatever the insurance unit is. In some cases the insurance unit may well be a township; in other cases it may be a municipality. That will be up to the province but it must be a sufficiently small unit so that the long term average yield in that unit is much the same throughout. In other words, it would be inequitable for the farmers and the governments concerned to try to have the same premium rate, for example, in all parts of western Canada in a scheme of that sort. It would not work; it would not be practicable. Therefore, we have to have some area which will be called an insurance unit, as I say, it may be a township, it may be a municipality, in which the rate will be the same. In that unit one of the requirements will be that 25 per cent of the farmers or 25 per cent of the acreage must be covered before we will contribute in order to prevent the scheme being put in a position which is not actuarially sound.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Can the minister say whether in any given province there must be a minimum number of units that come under the act?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: No. As far as the act is drawn a province could have one unit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: I wonder whether I might just finish these things because we seem to be going down various tracks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: I just want to understand what the minister said. He said that 25 per cent of the farmers within a unit must subscribe to the scheme and the premium must be the same. Does that mean the premium in the unit or the premium in the whole province?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: This is one of the reasons that you must have these insurance units, you might say, so that you could have a difference in premium from one part of the province to another.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: That is what I wanted to know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
We have covered two of these conditions which must be met for financial assistance to be available. The third is that they be insured up to but not exceeding 60 per cent of the long term average yield in the area. In other words, our 20 per cent of the premiums will cover only 20 per cent of the cost of insuring the crop up to 60 per cent of the long term average yield.
Crop Insurance

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Is it 60 per cent the cash investment of the crop loss that my hon. friend has in mind?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Now the hon. member is getting into the details which I think we should deal with in committee of the whole after second reading. There are an infinite number of details really which could be brought up and dealt with. At this stage I think it is desirable really just for the committee to consider the general principles of the scheme which I have just attempted to outline and not get into these very numerous details which could be brought up and which could be discussed, and many of which I expect will be. I do not want to give the hon. member and the committee the idea that I am trying to avoid any questions, but at this stage I do not think it is desirable to go into this because we could keep on actually for days on these numerous small points.
There is one other point that I should like to make, namely that farmers will not be eligible for both crop insurance and prairie farm assistance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: Oh!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: The Prairie Farm Assistance Act will continue in effect but a farmer who is insured will not be eligible for the insurance and for prairie farm assistance both. In other words, we would consider that the contribution made by the federal taxpayer toward the cost of crop insurance is one thing and the contribution made by the federal taxpayer for the cost of prairie farm assistance is another thing, and that the same farmers should not be eligible to receive both of these at the same time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
You borrowed that from the
Minister of Finance's budget.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
At the same time, the
farmer who comes in under the crop insurance scheme will not be required to pay the 1 per cent levy for Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments. In other words, he will neither pay into the Prairie Farm Assistance Act fund or will he be eligible to take money out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture indicated that we had before us a very complex subject which has had the attention of several royal commissions certainly in the western prairie provinces and perhaps elsewhere. As the minister indicated, we now have some experience to guide us because since approximately 1939 there has been a federal crop insurance scheme in the United States which has been revised on at least two occasions since then.

Crop Insurance
I believed, after reading the resolution in the broad general terms as it appeared on the order paper, that this would be the position we would be in. We had here the barest bones without any indication of the meat that might be provided in the bill. But having listened to the minister I am convinced we will find that there is going to be a great deal of vagueness and inadequacy in the bill because from the few remarks he has made it would appear there are so many provisos that I rather question whether very many of the provinces are likely to co-operate with the minister on something as nebulous as he has outlined to the committee at this time.
The minister indicated today that he had had a certain number of representations urging crop insurance, as many of us have, but from which provinces has the minister had anything officially in the nature of an enthusiastic indication of interest in connection with the kind of scheme he has outlined in the barest form to the committee this afternoon? We will reserve our detailed examination and comment until we see the bill, but our fear, enforced by what the minister has said, is that this measure really is window dressing and that we are likely to be faced with something which will be just an empty dummy shell. The bill may prove otherwise but no encouragement in that direction comes from the remarks just made by the minister.
One of the strongest supports for that assertion on my part is the statement of the minister that no farmer will be eligible for both P.F.A.A. and the new scheme of federal-provincial crop insurance. This seems to be entirely inconsistent with the minister's earlier assertion in his short speech that P.F.A.A., as the royal commissions also indicated, is not and was not intended to be crop insurance. The minister will be well aware that the recent commissions in 1955 and 1956 under the authority of the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan both felt that a proper crop insurance scheme should at least be complementary to P.F.A.A. What we fear, and we will retain our fears until we see some reason in the substance of the bill for changing them, is that the minister is really asking the house for a blank cheque with regard to something that was talked about in the recent election campaigns.
The minister has been in office for two years and has had at least an annual conference with the ministers of agriculture of the provinces. Which provinces have indicated that they would be interested in a scheme with the backdoor provisos such as he has enunciated? Was it the expectation of the government in introducing this resolution that it would likely

have some national application in the near future? I find that the only reported reference to crop insurance made by the Prime Minister in the 1957 election campaign which I have been able to discover was in a speech he made at Brantford on May 9, 1957. He enunciated his agricultural policy at that meeting and is reported by the Brantford Expositor as having said that he would develop "a more realistic crop insurance plan for drought, flood and hail in co-operation with the prairie provinces". I note that the resolution does not contemplate any restriction so far as the provinces are concerned, but from what provinces other than the prairie provinces, has there been any indication as a result of the two annual federal-provincial conferences held under the minister's regime that what he indicates will be offered in the bill is likely to obtain very early acceptance?
He indicated that there must be a minimum number of participants. I believe that was a recommendation of the Saskatchewan commission which made its report in December, 1956. They felt that they could criticize the undue voluntary content of the United States plan. The Manitoba commission pointed out that actually only 7.6 per cent of farmers in the United States are carrying some kind of crop insurance under the voluntary scheme and that in 1955 only 2.66 per cent, in terms of dollar value of crops, were insured under, as the commission reported, the excessively voluntary scheme there.
This seems to be a very far cry from the type of thing we heard from the minister last year and, indeed, from the Prime Minister. I recall that on August 30 last year the Prime Minister uttered ringing words about the possibilities there might be in this kind of scheme. He referred to providing a comprehensive crop insurance plan. In his remarks this afternoon the minister referred to an all-risk insurance plan but he indicated definitely that it might not apply in certain provinces in a general way and might apply only to one particular crop.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: That is entirely up to the province.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
In addition, the evidence before both the Manitoba and Saskatchewan commissions was such that neither was prepared to recommend to their governments that something of this kind be undertaken without federal participation in much more than half of the cost of administration, or greater participation on the part of the federal government than the Minister of Agriculture has indicated that he is prepared to recommend. In other words, the catastrophic losses that the commissions indicated were possible and which both commissions

said were beyond the financial capabilities of a provincial government would be met under the minister's scheme simply by loans, not by contributions. That I do not think is likely, having regard to the commission reports, to commend itself for early acceptance by the provincial administrations unless the bill has in it something different from what the minister has outlined.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
I should be greatly interested to learn from the minister to what extent provincial governments have shown interest in the type of legislation he has presented to the House of Commons this afternoon. I have taken a great deal of interest in the subject of crop insurance and the subject of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the past and I have always said that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be expanded and extended to specific crop areas outside the prairies in order to provide for agriculture, where crops face serious hazards, the same kind of protection as the people on the prairies have enjoyed under this scheme now for twenty years.
I have no knowledge of whether the Minister of Agriculture has consulted with all or a majority of the provinces but I would consider that this would be an essential requirement before bringing in such a bill. The minister has said that the federal government has not the jurisdiction to go into a scheme of crop insurance as has been presented here or as has been forecast here this afternoon. But the federal government undoubtedly has had sufficient jurisdiction to provide a scheme like the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which covers farming within a certain area. In other words, the federal government has had ample jurisdiction over a period of twenty years to have established and implemented a system of payments for crop failure to producers in time of loss. The announcement in this legislation, even though it may be extended to other provinces, shows that it is a restricted type of insurance. In addition to that, it will require substantial contributions from the provincial governments themselves. In other words, this is really a retreat in jurisdiction. Yet the minister says that in this retreat the government could bring in a proposition which would contribute only to provincial schemes.
In bringing in legislation such as that which the minister has forecast, I would think he would have had many conferences with the provinces, that he would have consulted each and every one of the ten provinces, and that before he would bring in a scheme such as this one he would have substantial support from the provincial governments that must embark on this scheme and
Crop Insurance
must provide for premiums to be paid into the plan. Other than that, unless this kind of consultation has been held, this would appear to me on the surface to be something of an invasion of provincial jurisdiction, although in a subtle way. By this legislation the government is saying that it will pay into provincial schemes if they are proceeded with. By providing exactly the same conditions, so the minister says, for each province, it means that those provinces requiring the assistance most-those provinces and those producers-will be obliged to pay the highest premiums.
In bringing in this legislation the minister has had the advantage of the various royal commissions and the various studies that have been made in the past on this proposition. The Saskatchewan royal commission has made far different recommendations from the ones contained in this bill. As a matter of fact, it merely advocated that an experimental and restricted type of crop insurance might be undertaken with the federal government meeting almost all of the costs and with the provincial government being restricted to certain administration costs and acting in an advisory capacity.
One of the earliest studies in the field of crop insurance was made by Mr. R. E. Motherwell, who was a grandson of a former minister of agriculture, a graduate of the Saskatchewan university and executive assist-tant for some time to Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, a former minister of agriculture. In the past I have paid many tributes in the House of Commons to Mr. Motherwell's work, particularly with regard to the study of crop insurance that he made back in 1944. I say again today, as I have said on many occasions in the past, that this was an excellent study, that it was a comprehensive study and that in general I agree with his conclusions, namely that the type of crop insurance scheme that had prevailed in the United States was not one which could be made applicable to western Canada with full benefits to all producers but rather in Canada- and I speak particularly with regard to the prairies-we should endeavour to expand and improve the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
In the province of Manitoba a royal commission was set up to study crop insurance and among other conclusions they had this to say:
(1)	That the 1 per cent levy now paid by Manitoba farmers to P.F.A.A. would be "quite inadequate to provide any form of all-risk crop insurance"; that, indeed, it was probably insufficient to cover P.F.A.A. payments over the long run.
The reason for that reference is the fact that in Manitoba the producers by their 1 per

Crop Insurance
cent paid in slightly more than they have received under the act, since the act became effective in 1939.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: And they said also that it would be inadequate to provide any kind of risk insurance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Yes. They said further:
(2)	That the yearly potential risk of loss in a crop insurance scheme, unless distributed over a wide geographic area, could be enormous even in period of relatively good yields.
(3)	That, although it may have appeared reasonable at the time, the earlier recommendation for crop insurance in Manitoba "cannot be successfully applied . . . under today's farming conditions."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: What date was that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
September, 1955. As I said
earlier, Mr. Chairman, I do not know, of course, whether the minister has consulted with the provinces about this legislation. If provinces other than the prairie provinces believe that this type of legislation will meet their needs, I think the legislation will be helpful to that extent. But as I see the situation, as an alternative to the type of insurance or the type of protection that we may have under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and particularly under an expanded and improved Prairie Farm Assistance Act, this legislation is most inadequate.
We have had the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in operation now for almost twenty years and it has a great many things to recommend it. One of the most important things to recommend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the three prairie provinces which it covers and in the section of British Columbia which it also covers is that within this area every single producer is protected. It covers everyone in the grain-producing area. Everyone who is covered in that area and who sells grain pays a small levy of 1 per cent. This means that not only is everybody covered but that, to make a general statement, there may be a few exceptions, such as people who raise livestock only and feed all their grain- everybody contributes by a 1 per cent levy on the grain that is marketed.
This, I think, has a tremendous advantage over a scheme that will not cover everyone within the provinces, and I do not think the Minister of Agriculture himself, who is introducing this legislation, is going to make any such claim. The United States has had a scheme in operation for some time. The administration costs of their scheme are borne by the United States government. The administration costs of the Canadian Prairie Farm Assistance Act are borne by the Canadian government. The administration costs of a United States crop insurance plan is equal to 25 per cent of the indemnities which

are paid out. The cost of administration, compared with the cost of administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, is excessive and shows that from an administrative point of view crop insurance is much less efficient than the prairie farm assistance. I think the administration costs of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act run to half a million dollars a year, or a little more, depending, of course, on the benefits which are paid out. The minister can give us the correct percentage, but I would estimate that our administrative costs are less than one-quarter of the administrative costs of the United States under a crop insurance plan.
In comparing, of course, the benefits which are paid out one would not expect that the Canadian benefits paid out under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would anywhere near equal the indemnities which are paid out under the United States crop insurance plan applied, as it can be, to the whole of the United States. One would not expect either that these payments would be anywhere near comparable to payments in the United States because their coverage does equal 60 per cent of the yields, and because, of course, their wheat acreage, while it varies as ours varies, is in the neighbourhood of 70 million acres, whereas our wheat acreage is more in the neighbourhood of 20 million acres.
After the United States had changed the type of scheme they were using to some extent, between the years 1948 and 1954, the indemnities paid to producers in the United States amounted to $136 million. Canada, with a scheme not paying benefits at the same high rate, and restricted to a smaller agricultural area and a much smaller acreage, nevertheless paid benefits, which I think are rather startling in comparison with the $136 million of the United States, of some $90 million. We have had a long experience under prairie farm assistance. I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that it has been a good act and today it is a good act, and I see nothing in the legislation which is presented to the house today which would influence me to substitute the kind of legislation that is being forecast for the kind of legislation that we have had, more particularly if that legislation is improved as it needs to be from time to time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext: You cannot have both.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
The minister said we cannot have both. There is sad news in the announcement that he makes, because it means for the farmers in the high risk areas, the farmers whose crops are subject to crop failure most often, that they will be able to get very little benefit from the general type of legislation that the minister has introduced. They

will be very hesitant to insure, and 1 am sure very resentful, to be told that in order to insure their crops under one act they must withdraw from another act. It would be just as ridiculous to tell the farmers on the prairies, "If you take out hail insurance and there is a widespread crop failure because of hail, we will not pay you prairie farm assistance."
That used to be the thinking, but after some criticism and some changes in the act the government discarded what was at that time a very bad feature. Coverage on the prairies under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in general is 100 per cent. At one time farmers could not be covered if they had another business or another occupation. The present Minister of Agriculture introduced amendments which allowed farmers who have some other income to qualify for prairie farm assistance; so in general there is full coverage. In the United States the coverage under their scheme is not nearly as great as it is in our country. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has provided payments to producers since 1939 up to the end of 1957 to a total of $204 million. The federal contribution to this scheme has been about half of that amount. Of course, as far as the provinces are concerned, they have paid in different amounts and have received varying benefits. The province of Manitoba in the history of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has paid in approximately $16 million and has received in benefits approximately $14 million. So Manitoba is the one province which has paid in slightly more than her producers have received by a way of benefit. Saskatchewan has received benefits amounting to $139 million in round figures and Saskatchewan producers have paid in $69 million, so we have received from this plan $1 from the federal treasury for each dollar paid by the producers. The province of Alberta has done approximately the same, having received benefits from the act of $50 million and having paid in about $30 million. Of course, the reason why Saskatchewan and Alberta, have received more by way of benefits than has been collected by the 1 per cent levy is because these are high risk areas, because these are the provinces which have experienced widespread crop failures and emergencies in past years, situations which have been considered to be national emergencies and in which the federal government has come to the assistance of the provinces.

hardship from time to time. The former minister of agriculture advanced the action taken by the federal government and by federal governments in the past as the reason why it must now accept responsibility in times of widespread crop failure.

Inasmuch as this legislation may be valuable to the provinces generally, we are, of course, glad to see it introduced, but in so far as it may place additional financial burdens either on producers or provincial treasuries while the federal government at the same time is prepared to withdraw the benefits of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, we think it is a retrograde step.
I make one further suggestion, and I do so in the hope that the government and the minister will accept it, namely that this legislation should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. Let us have before that committee spokesmen for the leading farm organizations of this country to speak for the producers. Let us have before that committee representatives of the provincial governments and provincial departments of agriculture to tell us how this proposed legislation may apply within their provinces. This, undoubtedly, is a step which should only be taken after there has been the greatest degree of consultation, and I suggest that since there are features in this bill to which I am certain provincial governments will object and to which I am certain producers will object, I feel that the government is bound, if it wishes the best possible legislation, to accept my suggestion and have this bill referred to the committee on agriculture for further study.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make in connection with this resolution respecting crop insurance. However, I have no intention of dealing with the resolution in all its details and my remarks will be brief.
When my colleague from Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) took part in the debate on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, he asked that the legislation be extended to eastern farmers. All the more so should this new supplementary legislation on crop insurance.
In January 1958, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) made a statement before the Canadian Agricultural Federation in Montreal -it is true that the minister was speaking on the P.F.A.A. at the time; but he nevertheless explained how difficult it would be to collect contributions if ever such assistance scheme were established in Quebec. To that effect, I shall refer to an article published in a Quebec paper, i.e. L'Action Catholique of July 23, 1958, which contains the following paragraph:
In this regard Minister Harkness answered that a crop insurance system was still being considered, but that considerable difficulties were involved in the scheme. -"Ever since I have been a minister," Mr. Harkness said, "I have repeated that the greatest single step toward improved farming conditions in Canada, would be the introduction of a crop insurance system. Studies are going on and I hope to be able to introduce such legislation before long."
And a little further on, the minister added:
"I may say that the result of this meeting has been to complicate matters even more, because a certain number of provinces did not show any interest in a crop insurance scheme. Some were interested, others less so and still others not at all." 66968-9-3321

I cannot disagree with the minister's statement, and I recognize that the situation is rather complicated. But since he has decided to introduce this legislation, I hope it has been thoroughly considered and that it will prove practicable with regard to all parts of this country, bar none.
As evidenced by the article I have just referred to, and following his meeting with the provincial ministers of Agriculture, the minister stated that some provinces were interested, others less so and still others not a bit.
It seems to me that the bill about to be introduced should be worded so that all provinces might benefit from it, according to climate and crop hazards, in the best interest of farmers. The fact has often been mentioned in Quebec at farmers meetings grouped under the U.C.C.; but, to my knowledge, no detailed study of the matter has been undertaken until now by the U.C.C.
The reasons behind this seeming lack of interest are said to be, first of all, that the P.F.A.A. was a very particular kind of crop insurance plan to which the federal and provincial governments were contributing. Then, the province of Quebec, with its mixed farming and its great variety of vegetable and animal production, was complicating the matter with regard to the administration of an act which benefits western Canada.
According to the U.C.C., tobacco and apple growers in our province made certain experiments. Insurance was provided by private enterprise and, of course, at the option of farmers themselves.
With regard to tobacco, and more particularly to cigarette tobacco, experience seems to have shown that it is possible, as the hon. member for Joliette-l'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) indicated; but even in those cases the rates were often prohibitive.
With regard to insurance for apple growers, since it is established on a voluntary basis, producers in the areas most likely to suffer from drastic changes in temperature were the ones to avail themselves of this protection, which proved fairly expensive and more or less practical.
Not only would it be important to consider the possibility of putting crop insurance at the disposal of farmers engaged in special farming, but it would also be important to put it at the disposal of those who are engaged in mixed farming and in a variety of vegetable and animal production.

Crop Insurance
In my opinion, this crop insurance legislation should include sections providing for a special credit policy in favour of farmers who are victims of damages caused by nature, such as floods, hail, tornadoes, etc. By such a policy a certain category of farmers, or even a whole agricultural area could be protected against localized damage.
In those specific cases, the legislation providing for such government credit facilities to agriculture would make it possible to grant the necessary credit with no interest charges to farmers affected, except, of course, to those who defaulted in their payments.
It seems to me that a clause to that effect would afford a measure of protection to a certain number of eastern farmers. Furthermore, such legislation could at the same time provide for the repayment of the capital, over a period of 3 to 10 years, according to the extent of the damage suffered by the buildings, or the various types of crops of a group of farmers of a given locality or area.
In my opinion, it would be extremely important that such a provision be added to the crop insurance bill which will be submitted to us shortly, because it often happens that excessive damages are caused in some areas through the vagaries of nature.
For my part, I am in favour of the crop insurance legislation principle, provided that such legislation be made applicable to all areas of Canada without exception.
However, in his brief remarks, the Minister of Agriculture indicated that this crop insurance bill which had been promised us requires some study in so far as its application in various areas is concerned. In my opinion, that legislation is actually a federal subsidy to the provinces, since the provinces themselves will have to determine what crops may be insured. However, we are in favour of this bill, although, as the minister stated, it seems most complicated.
Although the minister spent several hours preparing this bill, I would ask him whether he would not be prepared to put in a few more hours on it and, in that case, whether he could perhaps use that time in devising some way of getting the premier of Quebec to accept this legislation which would be of benefit to Quebec farmers.

with the various reports they had before them, was to say this about the Motherwell report, as found on page 13:
Motherwell concluded his report on the feasibility of crop insurance in Saskatchewan with this rather pessimistic comment-
The royal commission recognized that he was reporting on the pessimism of crop insurance studies made during the 30's. If the hon. member had read the Saskatchewan royal commission report carefully he would have noticed the following statement on page 5 at the bottom of the righthand column:
Crop insurance and P.F.A.A. were discussed at 16 of the 57 community hearings. The majority of the people in attendance at these 16 hearings favoured the establishment of a crop insurance program.
All the way through this report you sense the great need of people living in a drought area for help in the form of an insurance scheme to guard against some of the risk due to weather. We have supported this act and we have supported the amendments. But let hon. members who come from the grain areas do a little bit of arithmetic. This bill sets up a coverage of 60 per cent of average yield. If the average yield is 15 bushels, the coverage is for 9 bushels per acre. A coverage of 9 bushels an acre at $1.50 a bushel means $13.50 an acre coverage which you pay for partially yourself and partially by contributions of the federal government. The farmer of western Canada is not asking for handouts. He is not asking for relief. However, he will be glad that we are contributing half of the cost of administration and 20 per cent of the premiums because it is roughly the same as we give to the workingman of Canada. In the unemployment insurance arrangements for contributions they have had this since 1940. At long last, 19 years later, we give the same equal treatment to those in the agricultural industry.
I will just point that fact out to you, Mr. Chairman, in the hope that those who have the responsibility to carry the truth of what is happening here to the people of Canada will not let the type of comment made by the hon. member for Assiniboia get out across the country. I think the committee will recognize that this particular resolution, in principle,-I do not say in fact; and I do not deny that possibly the bill when introduced will have many features that will be highly desirable-is one of the most important matters to be put before this parliament at this particular session. I join with the hon. member for Assiniboia at once in expressing my regrets that this bill is being introduced at this late stage at a time when I am afraid the house will not be afforded the opportunity of giving the kind of consideration which this measure deserves. This is not the only important measure that is being introduced by the government at this late stage in the session. There is before us other legislation that should have been introduced earlier in the session.
This measure is one of the greatest importance. It is a bill that can provide the greatest benefit to the agricultural community of this country; but it is a measure that ought to be thought out carefully. It is a measure in connection with which we should invite the views not only of the provincial governments
Crop Insurance
but as well all the national farm organizations. This can only be done by having the bill sent to a parliamentary committee. Whether it be to the existing committee on agriculture or to a special committee, as was done in the case of unemployment insurance, I am not now arguing, but I do suggest, and in doing so I take advantage of the Prime Minister's presence at this time, that a measure of this importance ought to be examined from every point of view, and the only way that can be done is by carrying out the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
I do not propose to examine the historical features of the proposal because I do not pretend to have the knowledge that some other hon. members have on this subject. I have looked at the report to which the member for Qu'Appelle has just directed our attention, the 1952 Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life. I have examined some of its conclusions in the fourteen reports which were presented in December, 1956. I have spent some time in studying the report made by the Saskatchewan section of the United Farmers of Canada when they submitted a plan for all-risk crop insurance applying to all grain crops. I have paid some attention to the study which was made by Mr. Motherwell in 1944, who reported I believe as a member of the Saskatchewan reconstruction council on crop insurance, and to the study in Alberta in 1935.
Since no reference has been made to that, so that the record might be more complete, I would just mention that in that province crop insurance received consideration, and in 1936 a government committee report was issued suggesting three courses of action: First, an all risk crop insurance plan which would guarantee a minimum return either in yield or in value to the farmer; second, crop income payments; and, third, farm storage, that is sealed farm storage for grain in good years which would be available on the farms in dry years. Then there is the study in the Department of Agriculture itself when Mr. W. J. Hansen of the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture made a complete exhaustive study of this problem in connection with P.F.A.A. in 1936. So there is a wealth of material on this subject.
Much comment has been offered about the crop-insurance scheme in the United States. We should understand how that scheme is written, and how it is sold, and that certain types of crop insurance cannot be carried out in a country like Canada or even in that country in areas of low crop production. It could only be carried out

Crop Insurance
in areas of high crop production and therefore does not attack the problem which prairie farm assistance attacks in this country; and it should not be forgotten that they do not have what we have in Canada, P.F.A.A. I think if the minister of agriculture in the St. Laurent government has the opportunity of reading today's Hansard and what the hon. member for Assiniboia said about that particular measure, and associates with that what the Prime Minister said in 1958, Mr. Gardiner will feel that he has indeed at long last received from his opponents, none of whom was more vigorous than the hon. member for Assiniboia, the kind of tribute and acknowledgement which I wish the hon. member for Assiniboia had given to Mr. Gardiner when he was a member of this house.

The Prairie Farm Assistance Act had its inception through the vision of the Minister of Agriculture-*
Then Mr. Gardiner.
-and what has been done deserves the appreciation of those who live in drought areas.
When we are comparing the United States system of crop insurance, bearing in mind that they do not have P.F.A.A., I think that these words of tribute to Mr. Gardiner, who was really the greatest friend western Canada ever had in this parliament, will show that what he did constitutes a great record in the field of agriculture. I do not think there is any question that the present Minister of Agriculture must day to day be confronted with evidence which was not open to him before and which indicates what an outstanding minister of agriculture we had in the person of Mr. Gardiner.
When the minister introduced this measure today he referred to it as an all-risk crop insurance. I note that that phrase "all-risk crop insurance" is used in the Saskatchewan report of 1952, the one in Alberta in 1935, the one in Manitoba in 1954, and so on, but I wonder if that is an accurate description of what the minister really has in mind in the resolution he puts forward today. I suggest to him that this is not a proposal for allrisk crop insurance, and before I take my seat I hope to establish the validity of this statement.

The minister said that the government is confronted in the proposal that it has made with the hindrances and obstacles which are embedded in our constitution, and that the federal government cannot bring forward any other kind of scheme in principle than the one introduced today. I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that that is not the case. This may be the desirable thing to do, but if he wants to use the analogy of unemployment insurance he can follow the example taken by the government of Mr. Mackenzie King in 1940. The government of that day did not bring in unemployment insurance without consultation with the provinces. It had no power under our constitution to impose any kind of contributions for the purpose of unemployment insurance on the employers or workers of our country. It had to get that power from the provinces as the minister knows.

speechtext: I pointed that out.

Yes, my hon. friend pointed it out, but he did it in such a subdued manner as not to indicate that he was fully aware that what had been done in that case he might well have done in this case. My hon. friends opposite are on record as having promised the people of Canada a comprehensive system of crop insurance; the words of the Prime Minister are there for everyone to read. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River referred to the statement made by the Prime Minister on August 30, 1958, whose words appearing on page 4346 and page 4347 of Hansard for that date clearly establish, as the hon. member pointed out, that what the Prime Minister had in mind was provision for a comprehensive crop insurance program. That is not what is before the house at the present time.
Then because this matter is important, I put on record the words of the Prime Minister uttered in this house on September 6, 1958, to be found at pages 4747 and 4748 of Hansard. Here is what the present Prime Minister said:
When the next session arrives we intend to introduce a measure for which the farmers have asked from the earliest days in western Canada, something which has also been requested by farmers in other parts of Canada, an insurance plan to bring about the assurance of at least a modicum of income, that degree of income which will not cost the farmer too much to assure himself of, and through which during the dark days of drought the farmer may be assured of at least a fair and reasonable rate of return. That is one of the things that came about under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That met the situation in the western provinces to a degree. That legislation was placed on the statute books as a result of the initiative of the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. It has been expanded, it has served a successful purpose and has been beneficial. Farmers generally

are today asking for something further in that direction and it is because they are asking for that, we intend to provide the opportunity at the next session of parliament of taking this further step.
My submission to this committee is that what we now have before us is not the kind of measure which these general words of the Prime Minister indicated was in the mind of the government as legislation in the field of crop insurance to be introduced during the present session. The hon. gentleman need not feel inhibited by the constitution. If the minister wishes he can do what was done in 1940, when we embarked on unemployment insurance. He has the same course open to him as we had; he can have the provinces called together, he can ask for an amendment to the constitution and he can bring forward a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance.

What was done then was to pass an act in this parliament saying that the government of Canada was prepared to extend certain financial grants to provinces which were prepared to embark upon schemes having to do with the establishment in Canada of old age pensions. But that was not an immediately comprehensive measure and no one ever pretended it was. So the hon. gentleman is, I think, struck at once with one of the real obstacles in this matter, an obstacle which suggests that 66968-9-333

I suggest to the minister that it is not too late for him or for the government to take the kind of step which would present to the farmers of Canada a comprehensive national scheme of crop insurance.
If this is not done, may I point out that we have had from the minister no assurances whatsoever as to what the attitude of the provinces is going to be. We know that in 1958 there was a conference with the provinces. I think the minister mentioned that this afternoon, and the minister referred to this conference when he spoke in this house in 1958. But he intimated then that the discussions were of a general character and that no final conclusion was taken. The minister said, I find, on June 4, 1958 as reported in Hansard at page 829:
As a result of the recent conference with the provincial ministers of agriculture, Mr. Speaker, no particular consideration has been given to this matter. The whole matter, however, has been under very active consideration for many months past, and a considerable number of members of the Department of Agriculture have put a good deal of study and a good deal of work into the whole question of crop insurance and have prepared certain recommendations, which I am considering at the moment.
What provinces are going to enter this scheme? Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta? These provinces have, of course, studied this question. But what is the position of Ontario? I know what was said in the election of 1957 all over southwestern Ontario by those who now sit on the treasury benches. At that time, as very hon. member from western Ontario now sitting in this house knows, the farmers in that area had suffered very great economic losses as a result of crop damage by storm and we were told by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, among others, that if this government came into power, in co-operation with the province of Ontario under Mr. Frost, we would be presented with a plan for the compensation of our farmers either directly out of federal and provincial treasuries or by virtue of some legislation which would be passed. In fairness to the Minister of Agriculture I must say that I wired him after the election of June 1957 and reminded him of the promise made, particularly by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. I also spoke to the Minister of Agriculture on the telephone and he said: I am not commenting on that. I am simply saying that what you are now submitting is not the policy of the government of Canada at the present time. I do not know if the Minister of Agriculture remembers this. He pointed out what the constitutional position was; that it was up to the provinces, and

Crop Insurance
if they found it could not be done out of their own financial resources, if they found these resources did not enable them to take care of the situation, they had the right in that event to turn to the federal government. But there had been no such request made by any provincial government and consequently the Minister of Agriculture took the frank position that notwithstanding these promises I could expect, certainly for the farmers of Essex county, no such assistance as had been promised by hon. gentlemen opposite.
The minister has gone into some detail today. He has indicated that the federal government intends to pay 20 per cent of the cost of the premiums. The federal government has indicated-and I want to get this right-that where the revenue from the premiums is in excess of $200,000 the federal government will loan 75 per cent, make a loan to the province of 75 per cent of the excess.

I thought I had said that. And the federal government is going to pay 50 per cent of the cost of the administration. That leaves 80 per cent of the premiums to be paid. An analogy has been suggested between this matter and unemployment insurance, but surely the fact that the federal government is going to pay 20 per cent of the premiums leaving 80 per cent still to be paid requires further explanation from the government before the analogy can be regarded as complete. Does the minister now know whether any particular province has determined (a) to come in and, (b) if it has, what percentage of the premium it is prepared to undertake. Is it going to accept 40 per cent to provide for an analogy as in the case of unemployment insurance where that percentage is borne by the employer and 40 per cent borne by the worker, or is it expected that the whole of the balance of the premium will be imposed on the farmer? If that is the case I am sure that we cannot expect that there will be many farmers who will come in under the scheme.
I know that the federal government has no legal authority-and if it had I know that certainly no government would want to take responsibility-for whatever policy a province arrives at as to the share to which it would commit itself with regard to a scheme of this sort but surely in the light of the statements made by the Prime Minister in 1958 and in the light of his own assurances about the studies that had been undertaken the minister is not in a position where he cannot tell this committee what provinces are going

to come in and, if they do come in, what will be the percentage of financial responsibility they will bear.
All hon. members of this committee no matter where we come from recognize that the farmers of Canada have very special problems and if this particular scheme or a scheme like it will assist them in the great losses which have occurred from time to time we will all be very pleased indeed. But I think it should be borne in mind that all the farmers in Canada do not live in western Canada and that the farmers in eastern Canada, as was mentioned by several hon. members who spoke previously, have problems and losses from time to time. Sometimes those losses are comparable to those suffered by any other group in our country. Take the loss which threatened right in my own county to which reference was made the other day by the hon. member for Kent, Ontario, in the matter of tomato contracts. Take the great loss that occurred in 1957 all throughout southwestern Ontario. These were very serious losses to the farmers of that area. I suggest that a crop insurance scheme can apply not only to wheat but to corn, soybeans, sugar beets and all of those things.

speechtext: That is the purpose of this scheme; it will cover any crop.

In fairness to the minister I should state that he said that if a province decides to bring in any number of crops the federal government is prepared to the extent of its commitment in this legislation to be committed likewise. I suggest to the minister that if he wants to have a comprehensive scheme he has the opportunity of doing what the Liberal government did in 1940 and in 1951 with regard to unemployment insurance and old age security.
There is no question concerning where we in this group stand with regard to this subject. At the national Liberal convention which chose the present Leader of the Opposition as leader of the Liberal party it was affirmed that we support the extension of the principle of P.F.A.A. to all parts of Canada where it is desirable to provide emergency assistance and to provide adequate financial assistance to provinces which establish crop insurance plans. That resolution is an indication of our willingness to support a practical measure, one that will not prove too burdensome on the farming community and one which comes within the possibility of their acceptance having in mind what I think is the very desirable standard of measurement laid down by the minister, that the scheme ought to have sound actuarial principles.
It is significant that in the resolution before us we have nothing to indicate that this is a

comprehensive crop insurance scheme. On the contrary the resolution as presently drawn and the minister's observations in connection with it suggest not only that no proper system of crop insurance has yet been set up but also that no plan has yet been worked out in so far as co-operation with the provinces in the inauguration of a joint plan is concerned.
I suggest to the minister that he ought to give us an opportunity of giving this measure the most careful attention in the dying days of this session. This measure ought to be sent to a committee so that we can ascertain what are the wishes of the provinces, what are the possibilities of their acceptance and what are the attitudes of the farm organizations. If that is not done I can foresee what will happen. I do not say that the Minister of Agriculture will do this, but I am sure my genial, vigorous and highly imaginative hon. friend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will go from one end of the country to the other telling the people of Canada that this government has an agricultural policy second to no other government in the world; not only has it got a vision for the north but it has a vision for the farmers of Canada, and he will call as his witness the crop insurance plan introduced by that distinguished hon. gentleman, the present Minister of Agriculture, which plan no province will have supported. Nevertheless he will have given the farmers of Qu'Appelle, the farmers of Essex East, and the farmers of Kent, New Brunswick, the impression that this, the most vigorous government we have had in Canada, has at long last brought forward a crop insurance plan. These men, the farmers of Canada, will not examine the bill in the way that we now have the opportunity of doing. Therefore, they will say, "At long last we have something that is going to provide for us when we have crop failures as a result of acts of God, and the like; at long last we have something that is going to give us the kind of security we require. We have been maintaining the urban workers through unemployment insurance and now we have something for ourselves." The real fact will be that all they will have is a bill passed by this parliament in the dying days of the session without consultation with the provinces or with farm organizations, a bill that has only some value in that it adopts a principle which if accepted by all the provinces might give it some substance.
I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture using in paraphrased language the kind of appeal he used to make when he sat in the third row back here on this side of the chamber when he in his insistent manner used to prod the minister of agriculture of the day 66968-9-333 J

and sometimes even the poor, helpless minister of national health and welfare of the day to take a particular course. I ask him now to consider this. This is an important bill. This is the kind of bill that could do a great deal for the farmers of our country. But let us make sure it is the kind of bill that will do that. Let us not bring forward a measure merely for the sake of gaining temporary political advantage, for the sake of being able to indicate, in form at any rate, that a promise has been kept. The real way to keep a promise or to gain political advantage, I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture-

Someone said that I should know. Yes, I should know because I was a member of a government which brought down very substantial measures. P.F.A.A. was one of them. When I think of the criticisms against that legislation that were voiced in this house by so many members and when I hear the kind of tributes that are now paid to the former hon. member for Melville, the former minister of agriculture, who was the initiator of that measure, as the Prime Minister said, I realize that we did bring down useful measures and, as the hon. gentleman said, I should know about these things.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL SCHEMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the resolution before us is, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources pointed out, a resolution that is going to complete the plan for agriculture that was pointed out by the Prime Minister in August, 1958, then I think a great deal more information should be available in the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture than accompanied this particular resolution.
I should like to endorse the comment and support the argument made by the hon. member for Assiniboia and also the hon. member for Essex East that this legislation be referred to a committee so that some consultation could be had with those people who are qualified to give us the information. I am surprised, Mr. Chairman, that there has not been more consultation on a formal basis with the provinces before this particular resolution was brought before us. It is quite true that the people in my area could have received great advantages on a number of occasions in the past if this type of legislation had been in effect. But I think that much more consultation must take place before any indication can be given of what good this particular legislation is going to accomplish.
Crop insurance could cover a wide variety of natural phenomena. It could cover hail, flood, drought and many of the other natural phenomena, and each one of those could have disastrous effects in a particular area. In my particular area I can remember only one occasion in my lifetime when there was so much flooding that no crop was harvested. It was back in 1928. Since that time, although there have been partial crop failures in areas in particular grains, it has never reached the magnitude that it did in that particular year. It is quite true also that there are other small segments of the area which are affected by frost or by drought or by some other condition. I think this type of insurance could be very economical. It is the type of insurance which could cost the farmer very little.
I remember some of the arguments I heard when I was in western Canada on several occasions in the last few years. On each occasion when crop insurance was discussed during the provincial elections in Manitoba not long ago the farmer was more concerned with whether this was going to cost him more money than he could afford to put out for this type of insurance. I think it must be borne in mind by the Minister of Agriculture-and he may continue to forget this fact-that many of the farmers that I met that are receiving the benefits of the prairie

farm assistance had not the amount of money available, and they have not had it for some time, that would be required to cover the premiums under a provincial scheme. Many more considerations must be taken into account before this plan is implemented.
If the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources was correct-and I assume he was-that the Prime Minister is implementing an agricultural scheme to solve the problems of rural agriculture in all parts of Canada, then this must be part of that scheme and it must fit into the scheme on a national basis. If this is true, then why not refer this to a committee which will have the opportunity of calling before it witnesses from all parts of Canada who have the information. I think it is quite easily understood that there is a great deal of difference between covering, for instance, grain and potatoes in my part of the country and covering cherries, apples or other small fruits in the Niagara peninsula. There is no connection between these products. The amount of insurance that would be necessary to cover these two fields would vary greatly and in most cases they would not be suffering from the same problem. In one instance frost would affect the crop and in the other instance it would probably be a wet condition or not enough rain or some other condition.
I think the Minister of Agriculture must be aware of the fact that the great problem in agriculture today is not crop failure or overproduction but lack of markets and lack of returns for the produce the farmer is producing. If the farmer were given a fair and reasonable price for his product, if he were guaranteed this on a forward carrying basis, then I am quite sure we would have no reservation in accepting the fact that the farmer ought to be able to carry this type of crop insurance himself. But in the circumstances there are many farmers in my part of the country who are not going to be able to participate in any type of crop insurance unless it is paid for 100 per cent by people other than themselves because their income has been such in the last two years that they are not capable of carrying crop insurance at all. They will not be able to pay the premiums, or if they do their families will probably go hungry.
If the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is interested, as he appears to be, in this legislation for agriculture, then the major problem he is faced with today is not this piecemeal program of putting into effect all the Prime Minister wants to accomplish on a national basis for agriculture but it is the real problem of prices. If he is going to get himself involved in the

Department of Agriculture, then I think he cannot neglect also to use his influence to see that prices are maintained and established on a parity basis so that we shall know exactly what we are going to insure and how we are going to insure it.
There are many people who, if they want this type of scheme, will be paying on a crop that they have not the faintest notion what it will be worth by the time it reaches the market. I am quite sure that all hon. members have received letters from the fruit producers and the vegetable producers in the Niagara peninsula in particular where this problem is much more prevalent than it is in any other form of agriculture, where they are producing a high price commodity for a market which may not pay the cost of production when it is finally put on the market.
I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that it is going to be very difficult to insure this type of crop against crop failure if they are not even sure it is worth saving. In fact, it might be quite a saving to the producers if it disappeared before it reaches the market stage because the small amount that they will save will probably not be worth enough to make it worth while insuring the amount that they have lost.
It seems to me that if we are to consider this crop insurance program in terms of the much bigger scheme that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources implied had been envisioned by the Prime Minister and partly implemented by this particular legislation, then I think much more consideration will have to be given to it. My information arising from a superficial examination in Manitoba of part of this problem would indicate that in the main the farmers of that province are not going to give up prairie farm assistance for crop insurance. On the other hand, I know of no group in Ontario that has developed plans so far to implement crop insurance if it is brought into being under any scheme. I have talked to a large number of farmers and representatives of farm organizations and, having regard to the scheme now before us, I think they are going to be less interested in developing plans to put crop insurance into effect.
Therefore I think there is a great deal to be said for the request of the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Essex East that this matter be placed before the standing committee where we would have an opportunity to hear presentations by the various organizations concerned with the subject. If this does not come to pass, then I suggest that the government is not prepared to support this measure by argument before the various organizations and that members of the government, just as the hon. member for
Crop Insurance
Essex East has said, are going to travel throughout the country and say to the people that they have given them all they promised to give and that if they do not get any benefit from the scheme it is the fault of the province.
This argument can only be met if the Minister of Agriculture is willing to call a conference of the provincial ministers of agriculture in order to discuss this and other matters in a concrete way so that he and certainly the various oragnizations will have a much better idea of what is available so far as crop insurance is concerned. I think in Ontario we need crop insurance and have needed it for some time. It should be established on an actuarial basis having regard to the record over a number of years. It should also be based on the ability to pay of the farmers, the municipality or whatever unit is used because I think it has been generally accepted that those who are least able to pay are the ones who need help the most. I am quite sure that this will apply to crop insurance if and when it comes into effect in the province of Ontario. Those who need it are going to be least able to take advantage of it.
The problem of how to finance the scheme, how far it should be extended and the advantages that can be provided can only be solved by hearing representatives of the organizations and if the measure is passed in its present form it will probably not be satisfactory to the majority of organizations who would like assurance with regard to one thing or another. It will not solve their problems.
