Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was saying that the farmers on the prairies will resent very much the reference by the minister of northern affairs to the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act as one by which the farmers are given relief. I think one of the most serious faults in the measure as forecast by the minister is that farmers who wish to come under the act must forgo the benefits of prairie farm assistance. Prairie farm assistance generally is a program that has been accepted by the farmers of western Canada. They feel that as far as it goes it is a good program, and they will resent very much having to forgo the benefits of this good program in order to qualify for crop insurance as defined by this legislation.
One of the questions which might be asked is whether or not this is a practical scheme; whether or not in most areas it can be expected that farmers will take advantage of the program as it is likely to be brought about. The Saskatchewan royal commission on agriculture and rural life in its ninth report, which is the crop insurance report to which reference was made earlier, has divided Saskatchewan by way of example into three general areas where the commission has examined into the feasibility of crop insurance and the premiums that would likely have to be paid under such a scheme in those areas.
First of all, I might say that in setting forth these examples the Saskatchewan rural commission has said that the following rules as to insurance will apply. The premium unit would be a group of delivery points so that at a certain group of delivery points all the producers within that area who wish to be covered by crop insurance would pay the same rate. The indemnity unit-I take it the unit on which payments will be made-in time of crop failure as defined in the legislation is also a group of delivery points. So, according to this analysis, farmers would not be paid on the yields from an individual farm but the indemnity unit would be a group of delivery points. That certainly would tend to reduce the size of the premium and some of the administrative costs. The coverage would be 60 per cent of the long term average yield group.

The Regina region is one of the three examples used, and the Regina region is used as an area of relatively low risk. This is the land that according to the Saskatchewan assessment commission, from the standpoint of production of wheat, is the most valuable land in Saskatchewan. It is relatively free from crop failure, has level topography, is near to markets and so on. In putting forth this example, the royal commission on page 139 of its report had this to say:
The average premium rate for the Regina region would be .735 bushels per acre for an average coverage of 9.4 bushels per acre. . . . The average amount of protection per farm would approximate $2,754.
The premium would be $215, making a ratio of premium to coverage of 7.8 per cent. The 7.8 per cent premium in this example in the Regina area-and this is an area relatively free from crop failure-is to be compared with the 1 per cent premium under the present Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
The next area of medium risk is called the Hanley-Davidson region, and in this area in order to be covered under the same formula the premium would be 13.8 per cent. I suggest that a premium of 13.8 per cent is a very high premium. It is a premium which very few farmers are likely to consider they are in a financial position to meet. The chances of them insuring with such a high premium is less today than it was a few years ago because the price of wheat, the main commodity in the area, is lower today relative to the cost of production than it was a few years ago. As the cost-price squeeze continues and the farm production costs continue to rise while prices for farm products remain at about the same level, and in some instances go down, farmers will be more and more reluctant to take advantage of such a scheme, and would find it much more difficult financially if they thought it to their economic advantage so to do.
Now I come to the third area, the Swift Current-Shaunavon region. In that region it is pointed out that with an average of 170 insurable acres per farm, the average premium cost per farm unit becomes $169, the maximum coverage about $1,035, and the ratio of premium to coverage becomes 16.3 per cent. Here is an area in Saskatchewan where crop failures are widespread. Here is an area which is more in need of crop failure protection than many areas; and here is an area where it will be absolutely impossible, if these figures are correct, to insure farms because farmers will find it impossible to produce a 16.3 per cent premium in order to provide in this average type of farm coverage amounting to $1,035 when such a

farm, according to the same example, would have coverage of just under $700 under prairie farm assistance for a rate of 1 per cent.
I say in all seriousness to hon. members from the prairies, particularly those hon. members who represent high risk areas, that there is nothing in this measure to recommend it to them. As a matter of fact, in the areas where crop failures are more persistent this measure does not provide any advantage. The government would have been far better advised as it affects the prairie provinces to have improved and expanded the Prairies Farm Assistance Act to provide greater coverage to the people who do in fact have crop failures, and to provide this greater coverage under the very important principles that apply to prairie farm assistance. This legislation can but cover a small minority of the farmers of western Canada. It will exclude the majority of the farmers. It places an obstacle before farmers who wish to come under the act, and it is an endeavour by the federal government to transfer the bulk of the financial responsibility for protection in time of crop failure on to the backs of the provinces and/or the producers.
The minister has not quarrelled with the statement I made that the administrative costs in the United States have worked out to about 25 per cent of the indemnity. If that is the case in Canada, then of course the 20 per cent of the premium which the federal government is paying together with half of the administrative costs is a very small proportion of the total costs which will be involved.

Yet in spite of all this the government is endeavouring to transfer this responsibility at least to some extent to the provinces. The government hopes, of course, that by putting forward some kind of a scheme the demand for improvements in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act can be turned on to the provinces, thereby avoiding what is in my submission a federal responsibility. A great deal has been made of the position taken by the Saskatchewan royal commission, and as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out before the supper adjournment, paragraph 40 on page 97 is very clear. This is what it states:
Crop Insurance
Potential liabilities in crop insurance-even in a test program-are beyond the fiscal capacity of a single agricultural province. Federal participation is therefore essential. A federal program, moreover, would avoid the high concentration of risks which would inevitably occur in a provincial program. Administrative needs also make it highly desirable that the federal government assume the major role.
This is the key recommendation in this report, namely that even in a test program, and most certainly in a wider program, the federal government must assume a major role. This is where this legislation falls down, because it is endeavouring to transfer back to the provinces in 1959 a part of the responsibility which was accepted as a federal responsibility in 1930.
The minister of northern affairs in his speech this afternoon made an oblique reference to impending debates out in Saskatchewan. Probably he had in mind some reference to the Saskatchewan election, whenever that may be called. The minister of northern affairs seemed to suggest that he would like to debate agricultural issues with me. Nothing would please me more than to meet the minister of northern affairs on a public platform in Saskatchewan to debate the agricultural policy of this government, including this inadequate legislation which is now before us and to let the people who might come to such a debate at some convenient place decide whether or not this government has fulfilled its commitment to the people of western Canada and to the farmers of Canada generally, namely to give them a fair share of the national income. This legislation, instead of endeavouring to do that very thing, is a means of trying to transfer what must be essentially a federal responsibility back to the province.
Mr. Chairman, in the light of the fact that there has been very little discussion with the provinces I think that this legislation will be exceedingly disappointing as far as western Canada is concerned. I believe it will be considered entirely inadequate and that it will bar from effective participation the very producers who need protection most.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from the point of view of the long term welfare of agriculture I believe this is one of the most important bills which has been considered by the Canadian parliament. The importance of credit used by farmers as a supplement to their own capital has increased almost continuously during the last 50 years.
The increased mechanization of agriculture and improved technology is tending continually to enlarge the size of farm operations and the capitalization per worker in the farming industry. In fact, the increase in capital used in agriculture and the productivity resulting from this use has been very substantial in the post-war period. This tendency toward increasing capital requirements, both for fixed capital in lands and buildings and for livestock and equipment, necessarily enlarges the role of credit, not only for the operation of the economic farm unit as such but for the transfer of the economic unit from owner to owner, or from generation to generation.
In 1958 the Canadian farmer had about $11 billion invested in land, buildings, livestock and equipment. About 60 per cent of this investment was in land and buildings. In 1921 close to 80 per cent of the investment was

in land and buildings and in 1941 it was a little over 70 per cent. In other words, the investment in equipment and livestock has been constantly increasing. The investment in land and buildings as a result has been constantly decreasing, although the actual amount, of course, has been increasing.
In addition, the average farm size in Canada, based on occupied farm land, has increased from 198 acres in 1921 to 304 acres in 1956. In the case of the prairie region the increase has been from 344 acres in 1921 to 546 acres in 1956. This change in composition as well as addition to the total investment has meant that a young farmer to get started today, not only has to consider ways and means of obtaining capital for lands and buildings but usually has to have chattels valued at only slightly less on the average than the capital to be invested in the land if he is to farm efficiently. In addition considerable experience in farming as well as the use of the many advisory services available are almost a must in the average situation if the farmer is to keep up with new production and marketing techniques.
During the past few years, in addition to the findings of several royal commissions, both provincial and federal, the government has received many representations regarding extensions and additions to the government's participation in the farm credit field. There have been many statements to the effect that the existing provisions for farm credit, private and public, federal and provincial, do not fully meet the changing needs of Canadian agriculture. Suggestions have been made that the total amount of governmental credit might usefully be enlarged, that existing loan limits should be extended, that farmers wishing to undertake larger and more economic operations should be given special assistance, that many non-veteran farmers-particularly young farmers-could benefit from the type of supervision and guidance available under the Veterans Land Act, that additional government incentives be provided to increase the supply of private capital, and that other changes be introduced into the present federal government system of farm credit.
With the passing of farm credit acts in a number of the provinces recently, most provinces now have some form of legislation to make credit available to farmers. At the last session of parliament an amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act was introduced which had the effect of increasing the amount available to the Canadian farm loan board for making loans from $80 million to $120 million.

Yes. Oh, I understand what you mean. As you are aware, loans made by the Canadian farm loan board in the last fiscal year amount to close to $30 million compared to less than $10 million in all except one year before 1956. At the last session certain acts relating to cash advances and financing farm-stored grain were also introduced to aid the farmers' financial position.
Following a review of the over-all farm credit situation during the past several months the government has authorized the following developments in the federal farm credit system.
1.	The introduction of amendments to the Veterans Land Act which extends the lending authority of the director with respect to veterans established under that act.
2.	The introduction of amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act which provides for increasing the maximum guaranteed farm improvement loans.
3.	The introduction of a new farm credit act for which the resolution is now before you. As stated in the resolution, the proposed farm credit act provides for the establishment of a system of long term mortgage credit to Canadian farmers. It also provides for the establishment of a farm credit corporation with an advisory committee, the majority of such committee to be composed of farmers or representatives of farm organizations.
The proposed act authorizes the corporation to make loans on two basic types of long term mortgage. One type is for loans to farmers on a basis similar to that now being granted under the Canadian Farm Loan Act, except that there are extensions and additions to the lending authority granted to the corporation as well as making the farm credit corporation the successor to the Canadian farm loan board. Among these additions and extensions are included the raising of the maximum loan from $15,000 to $20,000, and the increase in the amount of loan authorized from 65 to 75 per cent of the appraised value of the farm lands and buildings.
The second type of farm mortgage credit makes provision for loans to farmers upon the security of farm lands, buildings, livestock and equipment provided the borrower is between the ages of 21 and 45, has at least five years' experience in farming, and the farming enterprise to be established with the aid of the loan is an economic farm unit. It also provides that supervision will be a requirement when the amount of such loans is above 65 per cent of the appraised value of lands and buildings. Supervision will be available to the applicant for a loan who submits an acceptable plan of operation for
Mortgage Credit to Farmers his farm. This plan will in effect become part of the agreement between the corporation and the owner and can be modified by mutual consent or abandoned when the loan is reduced to the agreed level.
The total amount of loan which may be made as a supervised loan to farmers between the ages of 21 and 45 may be as much as $27,500, or 75 per cent of the appraised value of lands and chattels on the security of which the loan is made, whichever is the lesser. Farmers operating under this part of the act will not be eligible to receive a farm improvement loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act except when the principal amount of the supervised loan has been reduced to less than 65 per cent of the value of the farm lands on which the loan is secured or $20,000, whichever is the lesser. The act also authorizes the corporation to provide supervision for any loans which may be made, regardless of the amount of security, if the borrower so desires.
The proposed bill also makes provision for the transfer of present capital and operations of the Canadian farm loan board to the farm credit corporation and for the increase of the maximum limit of moneys that can be borrowed from the Minister of Finance for use in lending operations from $120 million to $200 million. Another extension proposed is the inclusion of a provision for the corporation to determine the method of repayment. This will allow the use of crop share repayment when applicable. The definition of "farmer" has been widened to include cooperative farm associations and family farming corporations. It also provides that where a person has two or more major occupations, one of which is farming, the corporation may determine which of these operations is his principal occupation for the purposes of this act.
You will note also that the proposed bill provides, as in the case of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, that there will be no subsidization of interest rates and that the corporation will be run on a self-sustaining business basis so that provincial and private schemes will still have their place, thus allowing farmers their choice of agency. I can assure you that it will be the intention of the government to keep the cost to a minimum so that the cost to the farmer for borrowed money may be as low as possible.
A survey by the director of the Veterans Land Act of potential earnings on a sample of farms based on average efficiency at the present time indicates that the provision of capital to enlarge and establish an economic farm unit is of major importance. If economic farm units such as this are established they

Mortgage Credit to Farmers can pay reasonable costs for money borrowed and leave the individual with an improved position in so far as his basis of net returns is concerned. It is hoped that no individual capable of operating a farm business on an economic basis may be denied an opportunity through lack of capital to develop such business to a stage which will provide a reasonable economic return. Such supervisory assistance as necessary will be provided on a cost basis for persons who indicate, through their own experience, initiative and planning that additional capital will make their future operation an economically sound farm business.
Before agriculture became so largely commercial the rural prejudice against debt was to a great extent justified. Now credit has become one of the most important elements in the management of the farm business. Its use increases very much the scale of operations and investment open to the family with ability and some assets. Within the rather restricted size of the economic farm unit for most types of farming, the keener ability and the greater the assets of the family the larger are the benefits they may derive from the use of credit. Like the physical equipment which the farmer uses, credit requires the exercise of much judgment in determining whether or not to use it, in selecting the source from which to obtain it and in manipulating it to secure the greatest returns.
With reference to the discussions in this house at the time of second reading of the amendments to the Veterans Land Act, I would indicate that provision is made for the use of the staff of the director of the Veterans Land Act to the greatest extent possible by the new corporation. It is also provided that the present staff of the Canadian Farm Loan Board will be transferred to the new corporation. In general, it is expected there will be the greatest co-ordination possible between the various federal, provincial and private agencies in the farm credit field on behalf of Canadian agriculture.
In conclusion I would say that at this stage it is felt that the proposed farm credit act, along with the other federal acts mentioned above, will provide the necessary federal participation in the farm credit field. If experience shows that more is necessary for the improvement of farm family living, farm operating and farm purchase, this government will be prepared to give further consideration and introduce further legislation as may be deemed advisable.

However, I want to tell him that I am going to watch this situation very carefully. I was not satisfied at simply hearing through another minister that he would do it to the greatest extent possible. I want to say that I have no doubt that he has read, as have I- and I read it actually after my remarks in the house last week-the submission of the interprovincial farm union council with respect to farm credit in Canada. I know the minister has also read it. In the 22 pages he will find that there is a recurrent emphasis upon co-ordination and centralization of farm credit policy in Canada.
I want to say to the minister that I have not the skill that one has after spending some time on treasury board. I sometimes attended treasury board as an observer or as an invitee. However, I want to say that as a member of parliament like himself I was completely convinced that we probably would in the near future lose this appraising and agricultural and guidance staff under the Veterans Land Act unless there was coordination of all departments of farm lending in government. I was never more serious, although I have been accused in the past of being very light in my comment that $5 million might have been saved.
May I say that $5 million is $50 million in ten years. The figure I gave last week was that perhaps the Canadian Farm Loan Board this year would lend about $90 million which was almost the figure on the books of the V.L.A. administration. I have been critical of the minister in some respects tonight but I want to say that I am highly pleased that he saw fit, before the introduction of this legislation, to make available to all of us-I think in some haste because the report is dated March 31, 1959-the last report of the Canadian Farm Loan Board.

speechtext:
I should like to say only a word or two at this time. First of all, I want to say that I welcome the measure which is now before the committee. In the second place, I wish to express the hope that the farmers in the maritime provinces will make wider use of this measure than they have made in the past of the facilities of the Canadian Farm Loan Act. In the province of Prince Edward Island I would say satisactory use was made of the Canadian Farm Loan Act but I think it must be said that in the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia the use made of the farm loan board was

only fractional as compared with the overall picture in the rest of the country.
I hope that the farmers in these provinces will, as I have said, make wider use of this new measure and that they will also use it particularly to enlarge their acreage. Therein, I think, lies the main problem in our maritime agriculture, namely that operations are too small. Under this legislation it might be possible for farmers to increase their acreage and thereby make their operations more profitable.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF LONG TERM MORTGAGE CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I have just about three short remarks to make. It is intended to make full use of the Veterans Land Act supervisory staff. As far as the administration of this act is concerned I should like to assure the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that the length of term of the loan that is proposed will be thirty years. The maximum age for so-called young farmer loans is 45 years. That would mean that by the time the term was up the age would be 75 years and it is considered that is long enough. If the term were 40 years, it would make him 85 years of age and I think most people would consider that is too advanced an age to lay down in a mortgage contract on a package deal of this kind or of the kind that is proposed.
There is just one other point. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made the statement that he had understood me to say that supervision will be provided only if it is asked for. That is not the case. As far as the package deal is concerned, for which the maximum loan on land and chattels is $27,500, supervision must be accepted in order for a young farmer, so-called, to get the loan. Once he has reduced his indebtedness until he owes just 65 per cent of the value of the land or $20,000, whichever is the lesser, then he can withdraw from supervision if he wishes to do so.

speechtext: In discussing the Canadian Farm Loan Board provisions a year ago the Minister of Finance at that time, if I remember correctly, said that as far as he knew there would be no increase in the interest rate under the legislation. I have asked the minister to consider whether a ceiling of 5 per cent could be placed on the interest rate under the act. He has not commented on that matter. I wish he would do so. I think that an interest rate of over 5 per cent would be a mistake. I think it would place on the agriculture industry a burden that would be difficult to bear. I wonder whether the minister could give the committee this much information. Can the minister say what he expects the starting rate of interest will be for loans by this corporation? The minister must have some idea when the corporation itself will start functioning. He knows the history of borrowings by the Canadian Farm Loan Board and the amount of the interest rate that will be paid on that indebtedness taken over by the board. Can he assure the committee that at least initially the new corporation will begin with interest rates that are not in excess of 5 per cent?

I know the minister is well aware of the fact that the current cost of money to the federal government is in excess of 5 per cent. If you take the cost of money to the federal government at this time as in excess of 5 per cent, add to it a small 66968-9-334
Mortgage Credit to Farmers service charge and then to that add the cost of administration of the new corporation so that it does not lose money, you will get a very high rate of interest which, in my submission to the minister, will be impossible for the agriculture industry to bear. I hope that that does not happen, but everyone knows interest rates are going up so rapidly now. When we suggest in this house that a new high interest rate is a matter of urgency we are told, quite properly by Mr. Speaker, that this is something that happens practically every week.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT

speechtext: Because there is no policy.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CANADIAN FARM LOAN ACT

speechtext: We have had a succession of high interest rates. The government itself pays interest in excess of 5 per cent. Add to that a service fee plus the cost of doing business under this legislation, it is possible- I do not say it will happen because I sincerely hope it will not be allowed to happen-that you would get interest rates of 6 per cent or more and saddle farmers with the heavy loans which they need if they are going to have economical units. What you will do in effect is to destroy much of the value which would otherwise accrue by this kind of legislation. I will be speaking out, as will other hon. members I know in this house, most strongly if in the future interest rates under this legislation at any time should exceed the rate of 5 per cent, which in the words of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture back in 1956 is an excessive rate that agriculture cannot bear.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I only wish to say a few words in connection with this resolution.
The minister in his statement indicated that under present conditions any young man who starts out farming requires stock and equipment involving a considerable amount of money. Therefore I am encouraged to believe that it means a liberalization of farm loans. If this means the adoption of a liberalized measure which will enable farmers in need of assistance to obtain loans where under the present farm loan act they were turned down, then I am happy to say that the change is indeed welcome and I congratulate the minister for introducing this new act.
My particular concern about this legislation is the actual availability of provisions to the small farmers of the Thunder bay district. I know the minister would say that there is no discrimination in the matter of approval of loans to any farmer large or

Mortgage Credit to Farmers small anywhere in Canada. The fact remains, however, that actual experience has shown that the small farmers in my constituency have encountered almost insurmountable difficulties in obtaining consideration for loans. This is not the first time I have had occasion to speak on behalf of the small farmers in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. There are several hundred families living on comparatively small farms, some of which are models of agricultural development; others are in the process of becoming fairly good and prosperous units. There are some, however, which are on the fringe of undeveloped areas and which require assistance; assistance in securing capital to improve their holdings, and loans for the purpose of improving their buildings and the purchase of modern farm equipment.
This bill if it is to perform what it is designed to achieve should be so administered to give consideration to the less prosperous farmers applying for loans. The present farm loan board activities are so restricted that unless an applicant for a loan has collateral assets to the extent that he does not need to borrow he is politely told that his holding does not appear to offer the prospects of being self-liquidating and therefore a loan on this particular property is not warranted.
The farm loan board should also be directed to consider loans to associations of farmers for the purpose of establishing cold storage facilities in addition to the federal grant that the establishment of such cold storage facilities entitle the farmers to, which is now set at not more than $50,000 for any establishment regardless of the total cost of the plant. Another aspect of the benefit which this bill could perform would be direct financial assistance to prospective farmers, people who are ready and willing to settle on the land and make farming their career and life work. This assistance, if extended to bona fide immigrant farmers desirous of acquiring a farm, could mean a new era in the development of our sparsely settled districts of northwestern Ontario. All we would need to bring about a movement toward the land is the active encouragement and assistance of the government which to my mind would rank higher than any other vision that I can think of.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the proposed new farm mortgage credit board should include a member from northwestern Ontario, someone familiar with farming operations in the region.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Harkness thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-67, to provide for
the extension of long term mortgage credit to farmers.
